`claude-haiku-5-5` (started with the bridge's `--settings`), driven by `worker.prompt`, watched with `herdr-world dump`:
spawn, concurrent spawn, nested spawn, interrupt (a TaskStop: `killed` → `interrupted`), bridge restart (the same six
rows, same ids, from the files alone) and a resume after it, all one row per child. It found one bug, fixed before the
restart step: a SendMessage to a finished child is an `isMeta` record, read as no prompt, so the resume did not show
(decision 5). The interactive model sent `run_in_background` as a string, which Claude 2.1.302 runs in the background,
so no interactive foreground child was seen; the foreground cases are the `-p` recordings'.

Unverified, and left as the evidence shows: teammates (their calls, files and hooks); whether `SubagentStart` fires for
helpers; whether a user-level `disableAllHooks` or managed `allowManagedHooksOnly` silences `--settings` hooks (either
way the transcripts remain); a child whose root process dies without a result stays as its files left it (#20's "a lost
process shows as unknown" needs process evidence this phase does not read).

## 2026-10-18 — #24 (phase 3 of #20): native child agents on both board surfaces

The floor overview's page and its wall screen show each worker's native child agents (#22's model, #23's Claude
subagents, the Codex phases to come) nested under it, to any depth. Code: `game/src/world/overview.ts`
(`OverviewChildRow`, the recursive `OverviewNode`, `visibleRows`' `more`, `endedChildGroups`, `childSince`, the filter),
`game/src/ui/overview.ts` and `overview.css` (`fillChild`, `wireEl`, `NEST_MAX`), `game/src/render/overviewScreen.ts`
(`paintChild`, `wires`, `WALL_NEST_MAX`), `goToChild` in `game/src/app.ts`. Fixture: `internal/childagents/testdata/many.json`.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The shape | **One recursive tree for both surfaces.** `OverviewNode.children` holds nodes; a native child is a row of its own kind (`kind: 'child'`, key `child:<row id>`), built from `childTree(ChildBook.of(worker))` (its order, cycle-safe; parentage never derived again here). `OverviewSource` gains `children` (`WorldStore.children` fits). `VisibleRow.depth` is any number and carries `more` (per level, whether that level's line runs on), which both surfaces draw their wires from; `allNodes` walks every depth for the page's bookkeeping (present rows, group sizes, Expand all). |
| 2 | Where a child goes | **Under the worker that owns it (`worker_id`), whatever that worker is**: an employee, an orchestrator (its freelancers first, then its own children: the crew keeps its shape) or a freelancer (under its orchestrator, also from another floor or in Unlinked: `orchestrator → freelancer → subagent → …`). A ghost orchestrator's own children are not shown on another floor's page (they are on its own). On the all-floors page everything is a floor deeper. |
| 3 | Unresolved | A child at the top of its worker's tree whose `parent` is not `root` (`unresolved`, or a parent the list lacks or a cycle, which `childTree` also puts there) is `unresolved: true`: directly under the worker, but its elbow is **detached and dashed** (no line from the worker reaches it) and it says **parent unknown** (a dashed chip on the page and the wall, in its spoken label). Never shown as `root`. |
| 4 | What a row says | The provider's mark (`markSvg` / `markFor`; one without a mark says its name), the name else the type else `Subagent` (the type beside a name), the description (one line on the page, all of it on hover and focus; two lines on a phone), the transcript's availability after it (`transcript available`, `transcript pending`, `no transcript`), and at the right the state in words with its time: `running 4m` (since `started_at`), `idle 2m` (since `last_activity_at`), `completed in 3m` / `shut down after 3m` / `interrupted after 3m` (start to end), else `completed 4m ago` (the end alone), no time when not known; `unknown` reads **state unknown**, in the quietest ink, with a dashed pip and no time: never one of the others. Times are the provider's clock, as #22 sends them. A diamond pip stands where a worker's lamp is (filled running/completed, ringed idle/shut down, half filled interrupted, dashed unknown); it never blinks: only workers do. Rows are tighter than a worker's and one line high, so a long list stays dense. |
| 5 | Totals | **Workers only.** `total`, `countItems`, `cityCountItems`, a floor row's `total` and the header's `N workers` never count a child; children carry no usage and nothing sums their tokens (a parent's usage already includes them). |
| 6 | Active only | **A running child is active** and keeps every row above it (an idle worker whose background subagent still runs stays, as does its orchestrator); any other state is not (idle is reusable, unknown is no evidence of work). A hidden child, alone or with its worker, is counted apart: `4 subagents hidden` after the workers' words, never as an idle or asleep worker; the line is unchanged when no child is hidden. |
| 7 | Default folds | **Every group open, except an ended child's own children** (completed, shut down, interrupted: `endedChildGroups`): a finished child's tree folds into its row on the page (an `open:` marker in the collapse preferences once the viewer opens it, like #188's asleep floors, so the page now always reads `effective(defaults)`) and on the wall (which has no preferences). A worker's flat list of finished children is not summarised: the page scrolls and pages with the keys, the wall goes to one-line rows and scrolls and pages (`wallPlan`, `wallPages`, `wallCycle`), and Active only trims it. |
| 8 | Deep trees | The indent follows the tree for **4 levels** (page: 20 px a level, `--nest`, `NEST_MAX`; wall: `WALL_NEST_MAX`); deeper rows stay at the fourth, their deeper levels' lines sharing its column, and the page says `level N` on the row (and in its label) since the indent no longer does. `aria-level` is always the true depth. |
| 9 | Keys and activation | Child groups fold and open like any other (→ ←, Space, the chevron, Shift+→/← and Expand/Collapse all, at any depth); ↑↓ j k Home End move through them. Enter or a click on a child calls `OverviewHost.goToChild(workerId, childId)`, which the app answers with `goToWorker(workerId, 'transcript')`; #26 swaps that one hook for the child's own transcript (done: `goToWorker(workerId, 'transcript', childId)`, see "#26"). `t` and `r` stay worker-only. No new keys (`docs/shortcuts.md` unchanged). |
| 10 | Live | Nothing new was needed to re-read: every event goes through `App.applyChange`, which marks the overview dirty, so `child.upsert` / `child.removed` / a generation change refresh the page and the wall with no transcript open. The wall's redraw key (`face`) now includes a child's fields and every row's `more`; the page's row signature already held the whole row (now with `more`, which replaced `lastChild`). |
| 11 | Fixture | `many.json`: one Claude worker, thirty children in every state, nested four deep, one unresolved, one finished with children (the fold); its frames are `children-many.jsonl`. The rename `ov-row--child` → `ov-row--nested` keeps the nesting class apart from the new row kind. |

Coverage:

| Bullet | Where |
|---|---|
| Children under agents, orchestrators and freelancers, both surfaces, three levels | `world/overview.children.test.ts` "nest under the worker…", "on the all-floors page too…", "children-nested…"; `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "render under…", "the all-floors page…"; `render/overviewScreen.test.ts` "draws a worker’s children to any depth…"; `e2e/h24-child-rows.spec.ts` "three levels nest…" (page and wall) |
| Keyboard, expand/collapse, long tree usable on both surfaces | `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "keys at any depth…", "an ended child’s own children…", "a long tree…", "a deep tree…"; `world/overview.children.test.ts` "children-many…", "collapses at any depth…"; `render/overviewScreen.test.ts` "a long list of children…"; e2e "three levels…" and "a long tree stays usable…" (page and wall) |
| Unresolved under the root worker without implying a parent | `world/overview.children.test.ts` "unresolved…"; `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "unresolved parentage…"; e2e "a long tree…" |
| Worker totals unchanged, no double count | `world/overview.children.test.ts` "total, the counts, the city’s numbers…"; DOM "active only…", "a long tree…" (`N workers`); e2e "a long tree…" |
| Updates with no transcript open | `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "updates with no transcript open…"; `render/overviewScreen.test.ts` "redraws when a child changes…"; e2e "the board follows child events…" |
| Row content: provider, name/type, task, six states, times, transcript | `world/overview.children.test.ts` "a row says…", `childSinceText`; `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "a row says…", "keeps the six states apart…" |
| Activation goes to the owning worker | `ui/overview.children.dom.test.ts` "activation…"; e2e "three levels…" (seated at the worker) |
| Active only | `world/overview.children.test.ts` "#24 active only"; DOM "active only…"; e2e "a long tree…" |

## 2026-10-18 — #25 (phase 4 of #20): Codex subagents from rollout files (terminal path)

The second production source of #22's model: a Codex worker's subagents on the terminal path (not the shared app-server:
#27), from its session's rollout files, on **codex-cli 0.160.1, 0.162.1 and 0.163.0**. Code: `internal/codexchild`
(`Source`, `Listener`, the facts and their derivation in `book.go`, `Rollout` and `ReadTranscript`), `codex.Meta`,
`codex.ParseMeta`/`ReadMeta` and `codex.ChildFinder` in `internal/codex/sessions.go`, the Codex branch of
`usage.Session` (`readChildren`), `UsageConfig.CodexChildren` in `internal/server/usage.go`,
`transcript.CodexHistoryStart`, and the wiring in `internal/app` (with `-codex-sessions`). Research:
`docs/research/codex-subagents.md`. Docs: `protocol.md` "Codex subagents (#25)".

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Who reads the files | **The usage tracker's `usage.Session`, once per file**, as for Claude: it already tailed each Codex worker's root rollout, so its `usage.Children` listener gets those lines; with a listener set it now also finds the session's **child rollouts** (`codex.ChildFinder`: the date directories from the root rollout's day on, newest first, at most `MaxScan` files; a child by its first line only, `thread_spawn` with `session_id` = the root; first lines read whole are remembered, one still being written is read again) every `SubagentRescan` or when the listener asks (`WantList`: a spawn within a minute whose rollout is not read), tails them and sends their lines by thread id. Not the `Finder`'s metas: they are the root lookup's, keyed for cwd, and only exist for workers herdr reports no session of. Not a second tail: no other reader of the child files exists, and the root's is shared. The child files' tokens are **not** added to the worker's usage (the root's reading is unchanged; Codex root behaviour stays as it was). |
| 2 | How evidence is made | **Facts per file, keyed by explicit ids, derived anew after each poll** (#23's rule): each rollout's facts (its first line, its spawn calls by `call_id`, the threads its activity records name, lifecycle observations keyed by turn id or activity id) are kept by that file; the children are derived from all of them and only what changed is sent (a `Removed` for one sent that is gone). A file that goes or turns out not to be this session's takes everything it showed with it (#23's retraction, by construction). Every piece of evidence carries the thread id, so a row's id is its native id's from the first observation on: no provisional rows, no merges; `DispatchID` rides along when known. |
| 3 | Identity | **Line 1 only.** A child is a rollout whose first line is `thread_source: "subagent"` with `source.subagent.thread_spawn`; `native_id` = its `id`; it belongs to `session_id`'s worker (the root at every depth). Never a later `session_meta` (a forked child's line 2 is its parent's), never `forked_from_id`. Guardians (`guardian_review`, `source.subagent.other`) and any subagent source without `thread_spawn` are no children. |
| 4 | Pairing | **By ids only**: v2's `SubAgentActivity` `started` (`id` = the spawn `call_id`, `agent_thread_id`), read from **every** rollout of the session (a depth-2 spawn is in the depth-1 child's); v1's completed `spawn_agent` `CollabAgentToolCall` with one receiver (`id` `exec-<uuid>` as dispatch id; the exec output's `agent_id` is not read: its link to the item is by time only); a legacy `sub_agent_activity` `started` is a dispatch only when its `event_id` is a spawn call of the same file. Never by time, order, task name or `forked_from_id`. A `started` whose file is not read yet is `running`/`pending` (up to ~0.2 s, or until the next listing). |
| 5 | Parents | **The child's first line** (`thread_spawn.parent_thread_id`; when the top-level `parent_thread_id` disagrees, none: `unresolved`), else the rollout holding its `started` (root's: `root`; a child's: that child). A parent not seen yet leaves it unresolved until it is (the registry's rule). |
| 6 | Own records | A child's records with `ordinal < subagent_history_start_ordinal` (and a record with no ordinal when there is a start) are its parent's copied history and count for nothing: lifecycle, times, calls. Not `turn_attribution`: 0.160.1 writes none, and a v1 child's own turn has `initiating_agent_path: null`. |
| 7 | Lifecycle | **The latest observation wins** (by record time; at the same instant an end over a start, `shut_down` over `interrupted` over `completed`): `running` from a spawn record and each own `task_started`; `completed` from an own `task_complete` or the spawner's `completed` (per turn); `interrupted` from an own `turn_aborted` (any reason) or the spawner's `interrupted` (v2 `interrupt_agent`); `shut_down` from a v1 `close_agent` item. A follow-up is the same row going `running` again. **Tool-call status is never the child's**: `wait` items and outputs (also v1's that name the child with `agents_states` completed), a spawn call's status and `interacted` are not read for state. With no observation yet a child file reads `running` (just spawned). |
| 8 | What rollouts cannot say | Left as the files show it, never guessed: a child whose process was killed without a record stays `running`; `unknown` is never produced (nothing on disk tells "idle and unclosed" from "process gone"; Codex writes `turn_aborted` on a normal exit, SIGINT and interrupts, which covers the cases seen); `idle` is #27's (a shared server's: "#27" below); an idle v2 child has no close. Recorded as [U] in the research. |
| 9 | Which sessions | Every Codex session the tracker reads gets a reader, also one only its lookup found (herdr reported none): the registry drops that evidence until the hub binds the session (herdr reports it; herdr's Codex integration does, by its SessionStart hook), and the bind replays it. |
| 10 | Root recovery | `Meta.Subagent` adds "any `source.subagent`" to the old test (`thread_source: "subagent"` or a parent thread), so `FindSession`, `Finder` and `FindRollout`'s callers never take a child or a guardian for a root; checked over every fixture (forked children, depth 2, 0.160.1, a guardian). `limits`' fallback (`NewestRollouts`) is no root picker: it reads the newest `rate_limits` of any rollout, which are the account's, so a child's are as good; unchanged. |
| 11 | Transcript | `codexchild.Rollout(root, session, thread)` finds a child's rollout by thread id (`FindRollout`) and accepts it only when its first line is a spawned child of that session; `ReadTranscript` runs the Codex parser over it with `transcript.CodexHistoryStart(start)`: inherited records (the copied `session_meta` among them) become hidden notices, so cursors stay put and the version is the child's own. `sub_agent_activity` is a hidden notice now. Opening it from a client is #26 (done: the same first-line rule, through the session's `ChildFinder` and tail, with `CodexHistoryStart`; see "#26"). |
| 12 | Fixtures | Scrubbed real rollouts (`internal/codexchild/testdata`, README): the live runs a, b, c2, d, e, f-run, f-run2, two v1 cases and the 0.160.1 run, plus two corpus cases from real work sessions (the inherited-prefix trap, a guardian), cut to the records read and with all free text replaced. |

Coverage:

| Bullet | Where |
|---|---|
| Spawn, interact/follow-up, wait, interrupt and close resolve to the correct child | `TestCasesWhole` (every case: parent, name, dispatch, end state), `TestVisibleBeforeReportBack`, `TestConcurrentChildren`, `TestFollowUp`, `TestInterrupts` (SIGINT, `interrupt_agent`), v1 close in `TestCasesWhole` (`f-run-v1b`, `f-idle-v1b`: `shut_down`); smoke "spawn", "two concurrent", "follow-up", "interrupt_agent" |
| Child state never conflated with tool-call status | `TestToolCallStatusIsNotChildState` (a v1 wait naming the child completed, a timed-out v2 wait), `TestFollowUp` (`interacted` alone) |
| Nested children attach to their recorded parent thread | `TestNestedChild` (from the depth-1 file's `started`, from the depth-2 file's first line alone, the copied line 2 ignored), `TestCodexSubagentsEndToEnd` (`internal/server`); smoke "nested" |
| Root-session recovery ignores child rollouts | `TestRootRecoveryIgnoresChildren` (`FindSession` and `Finder` over every fixture: forked, depth 2, 0.160.1, guardian), `TestFindSessionSkipsSubagents`, `TestParseMeta` (`internal/codex`) |
| Fixtures from real rollouts, 0.160.1 included; supported versions recorded | `internal/codexchild/testdata` (README), `TestCasesWhole/g-a0160-v`, `TestInheritedPrefix` (corpus trap); research §6 and this entry |
| Real-terminal smoke with a spawned child, including bridge restart | below; `TestRestartRebuilds`, `TestReplay` |
| Existing Claude child and Codex root behaviour unchanged | `internal/claudechild`, `internal/usage`, `internal/server` (`TestClaudeSubagentEndToEnd`, the usage tests) and `internal/transcript` suites pass unchanged |
| Foreign, gone, second reader, legacy history, child transcript | `TestOtherSessionsChildren`, `TestForeignFile`, `TestGoneFile`, `TestSecondReaderTakesOver`, `TestLegacyActivity`, `TestChildFinder`, `TestChildFinderPartialFirstLine`, `TestReadTranscript`, `TestReadTranscriptRefuses`, `TestCodexSubagentLines` |

**Real-terminal smoke check** (`docs/research/codex-subagents.md` §8): a private bridge built from the branch and a
private herdr session (`h3d-xsmoke`, own socket and database, `-sessions '^h3d-xsmoke$'`, `-codex-run -`), one Codex
worker hired by the bridge (`gpt-6-luna`, low; v2 by its model metadata), driven by `worker.prompt`, watched with
`herdr-world dump`: spawn (the row ~4 s after the prompt, 31 s before the child reported back), two concurrent, nested

again) and `interrupt_agent` (`interrupted`); a bridge restart rebuilt the six children from the files alone (native
ids, nesting, states, times identical). The row ids came back identical on a second restart; on the first they were new,
because the worker's `/new` before the run had raised its `child_generation` (row ids hash it; #22's "Restart": a
client never keeps them across epochs). No bug found. The session was then stopped and deleted, the bridge stopped, and
the throwaway rollouts moved out of `~/.codex/sessions`.

Unverified, and left as the evidence shows: SIGKILL of the Codex process mid-child, legacy-history rollouts (no sample),

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What a menu is about | Its **operation**: the dialog's own lines from its top (Claude Code's rule at the screen's left edge, a rule inside a command being indented; Codex's first line, "Would you like to …" or "Folder access") down to its question (Claude: the line right above the choices) or to its choices (Codex), trimmed, **whole** (no 12-line window, no 200-rune clip), without a rule. Looked for up to the screen's top: not found, the operation is all the screen shows above the menu, hashed whole, and **not complete** (row 7). The harness picks the dialog's style (`harnessOf`); unknown, whichever top comes first. Only `permission` and `trust` menus; any other keeps #88's hash. |
| 2 | Incidental lines | Lines that only say how long something has run or that it still runs are not part of it, nor of the excerpt (so a ticking counter is no `worker.upsert` every read): explicit patterns, **each a whole line** (`incidentalRe`, `TestIncidentalLines`): Claude Code's "Background task running 12s", a spinner's one word and its timer "✻ Thinking… (12s · esc to interrupt)", "esc to interrupt" on its own, an elapsed time or a clock on its own, a "denied in 1:59"-style countdown of words and a time. A line with a path, a quote, `$`, `=` or a shell operator is never incidental: a command line that reads like a status line (`echo 'esc to interrupt'; touch /tmp/a`) is the operation's, on the card and in the hash (`TestMenuOpCommandLikeIncidental`, `TestCardMenuCommandLikeIncidentalThroughTheHub`). The incident's exact line was not kept; positive extraction (row 1) is what keeps an unknown one outside the dialog harmless. |
| 3 | Two identities | The **hash** (`worker.answer`'s, the game's too) folds in the operation's lines exactly as shown and whether its top was on the screen: a change anywhere in it, beyond the old window or past a long line's 200th character, is another hash (`TestMenuOpBeyondTheWindow`); a rewrap is another hash too (`touch a b` and `touch ab` must differ). The card's **operation key** (`notify.Menu.Op`) is the kind, the blocked spell, the choices' count and the lines joined without whitespace: a rewrap or a resize keeps it (`TestMenuOpRewrap`). The service keys a card by the operation and follows its hash, but gives it a **new keyboard whenever its hash or its native call changes**, not only when what it shows does (a change past the 300th character of a line, or `touch /tmp/a /tmp/b` → `touch /tmp/a/tmp/b`, which share the key, can read the same on the card): a tap answers only the hash its keyboard was shown with, one on an old keyboard is answered "It changed" and sends nothing (`tapChanged`; `TestCardMenuNewHashNewKeyboard`, `TestCardMenuClippedChangeThroughTheHub`). The operation key keeps a card; it never authorizes a tap. A tap racing a rewrap must be repeated. |
| 4 | Native identity | For Claude workers, the **transcript's pending call** (`transcript.CallTracker`: the main conversation's `tool_use`s without a result, their whole input, its SHA-256, the line's `cwd`, and the `permission-mode` line), not the `PermissionRequest` hook: the transcript covers every Claude worker the bridge reads (the incident's was not started by the bridge), has the `tool_use_id` the hook lacks, and is on disk 0.1 s after the dialog opens. A dialog is matched to **the one** pending call whose command its lines draw **word for word** (their words its words; a line break one of its spaces, or none where the wrap cut a word: `TestNativeOfWords`), whole, or (top off the screen) its end, at least 12 characters, or (a file dialog) whose `file_path` is its path line; none or two candidates: screen only. Its id (`Menu.Native`: 16 hex over the `tool_use_id`, the input's sum and the line's `cwd`) is **folded into the hash** (`bindNative`: when the screen is read, when the worker's calls change, a `worker.upsert`, and in `answer`), so the game's `worker.answer` is bound to the call as a tap is: A's hash never approves a known replacement B, the same command in another directory (`TestAnswerBoundToNativeCall`). It also goes with a tap, and `answer` refuses a tap once the menu is for another call; another call under the same screen operation replaces the card (`TestCardMenuNativeCallReplaced`). The transcript is read every 2 s, so a card may open from the screen and learn its call one read later (one edit), and the game's hash changes then: an answer in that window is stale and is repeated. A screen that draws two commands alike (a word cut by the wrap exactly where the other has a space) is told apart only by the call and the blocked spell. Codex approvals stay **screen-only**: rollouts have no call tracker yet, and keeping the shared workers' `requestApproval` params (`codexserver.go`) was deferred. |
| 5 | Truthful ends | A menu's card ends "Replaced: it asks about something else now." (another question in the same blocked spell) or "No longer waiting: it was answered elsewhere, or the agent moved on." (the worker left `blocked`, or a new spell), never "Answered in the game.": no hook nor transcript record says how a prompt ended (research §1). "✓ Answered" only when the Telegram answer resolved it, "✓ Sent … still waits" when its keys left the worker blocked (#88 row 6). A screen read that fails keeps the question for **five reads** in a row (`questionReadGrace`, ~10 s); after that the game loses it, but the card stays while the worker stays blocked in its spell, buttons and all: a tap is checked against the screen at the hub anyway. An answer not sent while the loop still sees the operation (the hub read it redrawn, the lane full, a read or a key failed) keeps the card and its buttons and says why; one for a menu gone or replaced ends it. The asks' and follow-ups' cards are unchanged (#14). Known limit, from #88 row 4: an operation that goes and comes back in the same spell (A, B, A) gets no second card. |
| 6 | Disclosure (supersedes #88 row 2) | The card says **what would run**: for a native call, its whole command, its description, its directory ("In: …"), the dialog's other lines ("It also says: …", why it asks when the dialog says), and in bypass mode, for an `rm`/`rmdir`, that Claude Code denies it unanswered after about two minutes ([D] only); else the dialog's own lines. Never the conversation above, the excerpt or the screen's question line. Every line is redacted (`redactLines`). A **carrier** is found as written: a password after `-u`/`--user`/`--proxy-user` (and `-U`) `user:`, all after its first colon; an auth header's value, to its word's end and on through its line to a quote; a secret-looking assignment's or long option's value (a JSON key's too: `"password":"…"`); MySQL's and sshpass's `-p`, any word of that command as bash splits it (`mysql -P3306 -e "a;b" -pX`, `sshpass -v -p X`, after a `\`-newline too); a URL's password, to the last `@` before its host's end (the first `/`, `?` or `#`). Its **value is the rest of the shell word it is in, as bash reads it**: outside quotes a backslash escapes the next character (`\ `, `\"`); `'…'` has no escapes; `"…"` ends only at an unescaped `"` (`\"`, `\\`, `\$`, `` \` ``); `$'…'` only at an unescaped `'`; runs side by side are one word (`a"b c"'d e'$'f\' g'`); a value that starts inside a quoted argument (`-d "password=a b"`, `-H 'Authorization: Bearer …'`) reads on to that quote's end. An operation's lines are **read as one text**: a quote or a backslash at a line's end goes on to the next line (a newline inside quotes, a line continuation) and each line of the password shows `[key]`, the lines kept. **Every carrier is found in that text as it is**, and what they all hide is hidden at once, so one carrier's hiding never keeps another from being found (on the screen a password at a line's end hides the next line's first word, the next command's name, and that command's `-p` still goes). The text is read once: bash's reading from each character in each quote is a table made in one pass from the end, and each command name's words are read on only to a word another name's reading reached, so redacting costs as much as the text is long, however many carriers it has. **Fail closed**: a quote or a backslash left open (a command cut, a line cut) hides everything to the end of the command; a value's quote is read both from the text's start and from its own line's, and the farther end wins (a stray quote on an earlier line, in prose or a heredoc, then hides more of a value outside quotes, not less). On the screen a line break may be the screen's wrap inside a word, so a word at a line's end goes on into the next line's first word (that word is hidden too when it was a real newline); the native command's line breaks are its own newlines. Only the first 16 KiB of the text are read (far more than a card shows; the hub renders it itself): the lines after are `[key]`, the word that goes past them is hidden (a token `digest.Scrub` would know only whole), and a value that reaches them is hidden to them as one left open. Not read: `$(…)`, backticks and `${…}` are not parsed apart (a quote inside one counts as the word's), and a carrier's own name and separator are found only as written (in `$'…'`, a backslash where `-u`'s colon or a URL's `@` could be counts as one). Tests: `TestRedactLine`, `TestRedactLineQuoted`, `TestRedactLineEscaped`, `TestRedactLines`, `TestRedactLinesCarrierAfterCarrier`, `TestRedactLinesBounded`; cost: `TestRedactTextLinear` (eight times a hostile text costs about eight times as much), `TestNativeAboutCost` (a 60 KB native command costs what 16 KiB does); through the service to `FakeChannel`, from the screen and from the native call, `TestCardMenuEscapedPassword`, `TestCardMenuPasswordShellWords` (every carrier with every form, the open ones, commands over lines, wraps: no piece of the password on the card), `TestCardMenuPasswordAfterPassword` and `TestCardMenuPasswordPairs` (every two carriers on two lines and on one); through the hub `TestCardMenuQuotedPasswordThroughTheHub`, `TestCardMenuEscapedPasswordThroughTheHub`. Then each line goes through `digest.Scrub` (a URL's password, GitHub and AWS keys, JWTs, bearer tokens, key-shaped strings), is cut at 300 characters, at most 24 lines in all (a cut line among them: `TestNativeAboutBounded`) and 1800 characters, the rest counted; a dialog whose top is off the screen says only its end is shown. **Not configurable**: the issue asked for it, it is what makes a phone approval possible, and it rides on Allow replies, whose copy now says the command is sent; a secret no pattern knows can still leave, which that copy says too. |
| 7 | Partial operations | A permission dialog whose top is off the screen and whose call is not known gets **no button for a choice that approves** (a label starting with "Yes"): approving "a command that ends like this" could approve another one ending alike; its No stays, and the card says to approve in the game. Its native call, once matched, makes it whole and the buttons come back. A trust dialog keeps both (a folder, no command). The game's `worker.answer` is held to the same rule: `answer` refuses a choice that approves such a dialog unless its call is known (`invalid_state`, "approve it in its terminal"), its No and a cancel go; and its hash covers all the screen shows of it, so a change far up the screen is stale (`TestAnswerPartialDialog`, `TestMenuOpPartialHashesAllShown`). |
| 8 | The send budget | Per destination (the paired chat), `notify.Limits`, defaults: **pacing** of every call to Telegram but a tap's answer and the test message (a message, a card, an edit, a button change, a reply prompt, an answer, a reaction, every retry): a bucket of **5**, refilled **one a second** (Telegram's private-chat pace; a burst so an ask's alert and its four cards go together), and a 429's `retry_after` pauses them all. **At most 10 alerts and new cards a rolling minute** (ours, stricter than Telegram; silent ones count), **one alert per worker a minute**, either kind (a done after a prompt can wait up to a minute: one flapping worker cannot ring every few seconds), and **3 new card sets per worker a minute**. What does not fit is parked, one alert and one card set per worker, the latest replacing the earlier (`coalesced`), and sent when it fits only if the worker is still at it (the same episode; the same question), else dropped: no backlog after a resolution. A needs-you alert held by its worker's minute still opens its card (the card draws on the budget, not the alert's minute); the alert itself follows at the minute if the worker still waits. A card set goes whole or waits whole. **A message counts from when it is sent**, not let in: let in, it holds its slot (and its worker's alert minute or card-set place) while it waits on the pace, a 429's pause or a retry, counts from its last attempt (a send that fails keeps its slot), and gives it back if it never goes; what waits on held slots is tried again a second later (`TestBudgetCountsSends`, `TestLimiterCountsSends`). An alert let in is checked against its worker's episode before every attempt, after every wait, and dropped if it ended (`notify.send` code `obsolete`; `TestBudgetObsoleteRetryDropped`): no obsolete alert from the queue or a retry. A replaced card ends when the new one goes; if that one waits, the old says "Its next card follows within a minute (too many messages lately)." A restart replays nothing (workers first seen are known silently; nothing parked survives). Paced calls run on the replier goroutine, so a tap's answer (never paced) can wait behind a few seconds of paced card work, inside Telegram's ~15 s. |
| 9 | Diagnostics | `notify.menu` when a menu's card ends: where its identity was from (`native`, `screen`), whether approving was withheld, how often its hash changed under one operation (`redraws`), how many operations its spell asked about (`spell_ops`) and how it ended: identity churn (redraws, one op) and real replacement (`replaced`, several ops) read apart. `notify.limit` when a parked alert or card set goes or is dropped: cause (`cooldown`, `budget`, `worker_cards`), how many states it coalesced. No text, command, hash or label in either. |
| 10 | AI assessment | **Evaluated, shipped unwired** (`internal/approval`, `TestApprovalIsNotWired`; no setting, no protocol). The supported native path would be the same answer lane a tap takes (`queueAnswer` with the card's hash and native id, the screen read again), never a `PreToolUse` allow (it cannot approve a critical-path removal) and not, this round, a deciding `PermissionRequest` hook (the bridge's hooks only observe, #23 row 6; it would cover only the workers the bridge starts; a hook's deny wins and its timeout leaves the prompt). The prototype: rules first (off by default, an operation not whole, not Bash, any removal, move or copy over, truncating redirection, escalation, history rewrite, force push or fetched/evaluated code: ask-human, no model call), then the configured LLM once per native operation (a second caller waits for the first's verdict; verdicts are kept by id, never evicted, and past 4096 operations a new one is ask-human without a call: `TestOneAssessmentWhileAsked`, `TestOneAssessmentEver`), within a 20 s timeout and 30 calls an hour, its data nonce-delimited and the command as its card shows it; its answer must be exactly `{"decision": "allow" | "deny" | "ask-human", "reason"}`, anything else ask-human. An allow may only pick the choice labelled exactly "Yes", never one that also changes the agent's permissions ("Yes, and don't ask again …"). For the incident's command (`S=…; D=$S/…/scratch; rm -f $D/*; …`) the rules alone answer ask-human: an unresolved deletion target is a person's, as Claude Code itself keeps it. |

Coverage:

|---|---|
| The issue's ticking-context screen: one stable actionable card, no "Answered in the game", one alert | `internal/server` `TestPermissionCardStableThroughTickingContext` (the issue's own screen, Claude's dialog, the frozen control; the real path `parseQuestionOf` → `notifyFacts` → `menuFacts` → `notify.Service` on its default budget, two seconds a read), `TestMenuOpTickingContext`; `internal/notify` `TestCardMenuOneCardThroughRedraws` |

| Counts without text | `TestCardMenuRowsHoldNoText`, `TestBudgetDistinctOps`, `TestBudgetCooldownTwoSpells` |

## 2026-10-18 — #108 round 1: prompt secrets reviewed before worker.prompt sends them

Round 1 of 5 (bridge core): the detector, the review contract, the private files and their owners, the switch, and
`worker.prompt` (with its `/handoff`, Claude's typed and Codex's `agent prompt` paths) and Telegram replies. Rounds
2–5 wire the other routes (hire, run.prepare/start, schedules, presets, packup.detect, hire.interpret, answers,
wrap-up, handoff), the game's review dialog and drafts, and reconnect, revoke and child-agent leases. Code:
`internal/promptsecret` (the leaf: `gitleaks.go`, the generated `gitleaks_rules.go` with `LICENSE-gitleaks.txt`,
`structural.go`, `scan.go`, `offsets.go`, `review.go`), `tools/secretrules` (the generator and the parity check, its
own module), `internal/secretfiles`, `internal/store/promptsecrets.go`, `internal/server/promptsecrets.go` (the gate,
`queueReviewedPrompt`, `protectText`; `planPrompt` in `input.go` is `queuePrompt`'s checks, shared), the protocol in
`docs/protocol.md` "Prompt secrets".

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Detector | **Gitleaks v8.30.1's default rules, generated** into Go tables (`make secret-rules`: Gitleaks' own Viper load and `Translate`, the TOML's SHA-256 in the header; generation fails on `required`, `skipReport`, `extend`, a path rule matching an empty path, or any unknown field) and run with the standard library's `regexp` as `DetectString` runs them (lowercase keyword prefilter, LF trim and re-match, secret group or first non-empty group, entropy strictly above the threshold with upstream's rune-over-byte formula, global then rule allowlists with targets, stopwords and AND/OR, the generic same-line filter with upstream's `location()` quirks); the five path rules are left out (a prompt has no path); **plus our structural rules** (`structural.go`'s families); and, around Gitleaks (its code untouched), its provider rules that ask for a blank, a quote or the end after the token run again where a sentence's punctuation (`.` `,` `:` `!` `?` `)`) follows a token-like word (14 bytes or more, with a digit, an `_` or both cases), over a copy with that punctuation blanked, from 256 bytes before the token's word to the punctuation, however long the token (`punctuated`: `Use sk_live_….` and `(hf_…).` propose the token, as does a 3 KB JWT ending a sentence; the tuning round's class 1; review T5: a look-back of 1 KiB from the punctuation missed a long JWT); a colon alone counts too, at a line's end and before more words (`retry with token (hf_…:`: E2, which review T5's "colons alone only at the text's end" had missed), and where it may be a name's instead (a word of 14 bytes or more follows it: `adafruit_io_key: k3jd….`, whose keyword rule needs that colon), the keyword rules (the 99 with Gitleaks' name-to-value separator, the only rules that read a colon: `TestPunctColonRules`) run again over a second copy that keeps it, a finding there counting when it ends at the run after the word that colon leads to. No new module in the bridge's `go.mod`. **Parity**: `make secret-rules-parity` runs Gitleaks' `DetectString` and the generated rules over the pilot corpus, every static sample in Gitleaks' rule sources, those joined on one line and over lines, and targeted inputs: 5,395 inputs, 518 findings, identical (rule, secret, byte range) sets; the oracle's byte ranges are found again by replaying each finding's rule (match, secret, line and column must agree). The equality of an entropy at its threshold is a unit test (no sample hits it). Pilot corpus (development evidence, not a holdout): the generated rules alone 18/36 exact (the research's figure), the whole scan 34/36 with 1/22 clean prompts flagged; the two misses are unlabeled values (manual marking), the flagged one is the deliberate `api_key="example"` (row 4). Warm scan of a 16 KiB prompt: about 19 ms median (i7-10750H, shared; the tuning round took it from about 23 ms, `BenchmarkScan16KiB` from 30 to 28 ms and `BenchmarkScan16KiBReferences` from 75 to 72 ms, as the header and URL detectors' regexps now run only when their literal, `authorization`, `bearer`, `://` or `=`, is in the text); the rules compile on the first scan, so nothing runs while the switch is off. |
| 2 | Deviations from Gitleaks | `gitleaks:allow` on a line suppresses nothing (a prompt is not a reviewed source file); a finding whose secret is empty (an unmatched capture group) is no candidate; every finding keeps its own occurrence's byte range (never a search for its text). |
| 3 | Overlaps | Candidates never overlap. The same range found by several detectors is one candidate with every kind. Of overlapping ranges the lower rank wins: **a provider rule's exact format** (a Gitleaks rule whose id has no "generic"), then the structural families in this order: `pem`, `auth-header`, `url-password`, `url-query`, `assignment`, `yaml-block`, `prose`, `fenced` (a value's own boundary: quotes, blanks), then **Gitleaks' generic rules**, then `repeat`; then the earlier start, then the longer range (a span that owes its match to an own reference ranks after all of these: row 6). A span that loses keeps nothing, but (`kept`): when every span that beat it lends, it keeps each part no winner has, as candidates of its own with its kinds. A winner lends when it is borrowed (row 6), or when the loser is a structural value that runs into an own reference and the winner lies inside it with its own range clear of every reference (a complete token, a header's credential, a URL's password typed whole in the value: row 6). And when **a provider's format wins strictly inside a whole value** that runs into no reference (`auth-header`, `assignment`, `prose`), the value's bytes glued after the format (to a blank or an escape's backslash) stay proposed, as a candidate of their own with the value's kinds, unless they start a list's next item, a URL's query or path or an escape (`,` `;` `&` `/` `?` `#` `\`) or are only a sentence's punctuation. So `token=ghp_…,extra` proposes the token alone, `Authorization: Bearer ghp_…!tail9` proposes `ghp_…` and `!tail9`, `the token is https://…?access_token=ghp_…&x=1` the token alone, and `api_key = "Xk29fLq0ZrMv8;tail"` the whole quoted value where the generic rule stopped at `;` (`TestScanOverlaps`, `TestScanRecall`). Tuning round, class 2: a provider-shaped prefix cut a value short and its rest was never proposed. |
| 4 | What is a candidate | Credential-like names: the last part (split at separators and camelCase) is password, passwd, pwd, pass, passphrase, pw, secret, token, auth, apikey, accesskey, secretkey, privatekey, authkey, or `key` after api, access, secret, private, client, auth, encryption, signing, master, app, account, service, … or it ends in password, passwd, passphrase, token or secret (`PGPASSWORD`); never `max_tokens`, `token_limit`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `secretName`, `author`. Prose: a password word (a few languages) and a value with a digit or a symbol, or quoted; a key, token, secret or credential word and a token-like value (8 bytes with a digit; 16 without a copula); the copula may be `is`, `was`, `is now`, `was set to`, `has been changed to`, … (`` the password was set to `example` `` proposes `example`). A quoted value a few words after the word (or a comma) and a copula or a colon is one too (`the password used by the job is «…»`, `the password in these quotes, including the last character: "…"`, `The literal password, including its punctuation, is «…»`), when the credential word is the sentence's subject: the word after it is a preposition, a determiner, a pronoun, an adverb, a participle or a comma (`the token we rotated is "…"`), never another noun it modifies (`The password comparison result is "invalid-password"`, `The password check is "not-found"`, `The secret identifier is "request-12345"`: review T2); when the value is shaped like one (no blank; a letter and a digit or a symbol; a key word's token-like) and names nothing (one-case words joined by `-` `_` `.`, a credential name: `"DB_PASSWORD"`, `"invalid-password"`); and never after words that name what a password has (`field`, `policy`, `message`, `name`, `result`, `status`, …) or after a second copula (`the key is only ever sent to "…"`). A line of one value that a later sentence names is one when the sentence ends on the credential word (`The preceding line is the actual deployment password.`, the line above, our API token, the first line), never a relation it begins (`the key to reproducing this issue`, `the token check`: review T3), never a bare key, token, secret or credential word (`is the key.`), and never code (the line is unquoted: `validateToken(user123)`). curl's `-u user:password` (and `--user`), an option word after a `curl` word of its own command (no unquoted `|` `;` `&` `(` `)` between: a quoted URL's `&` is an argument's, review T1; `sudo curl`, `(curl`, `TOKEN=$(curl …)`, Markdown's `` `curl …` ``, never `"curl"` in quotes), never one inside a quote, `${…}` or `$[…]`: the password, never a placeholder (a credential word, `user:pass`, or one in brackets) nor what the shell computes there. One reader decides that for curl's password and a header's credential (review T4 (p2), T3P-1, T4P-1): it reads each line from its start as bash does (`'…'` as is; `"…"` and `$'…'` with backslash escapes; a backslash outside them escaping the next byte), an expansion or a backquote read to its close with its own quotes, blanks and operators nested inside (`${…}`, `$(…)`, `$((…))`, `$[…]`, backquotes, which close at their next unescaped backquote whatever quotes come between), what `$(…)` and backquotes hold being a command list of its own (so Markdown's `` Run `curl -u u:pw` `` and a Go raw string's curl propose `pw`), so a word ends only at an unquoted blank or `;` `|` `&` `<` `>` `(` `)` outside them all, and a line at a newline no backslash continues (a newline inside a quote or an expansion ends its line with it open: each line is read as typed); a value with any byte the shell computes is no candidate, one whose bytes it all keeps is proposed as typed. Its bounds (review T4P-1: 32 KiB of `curl -u u:$$$(` nested took 10 s): one pass over the text, nesting kept on a stack, each byte read once (a backquoted command's twice: its close first), never again per option or header; an option inside a password word already read is that word's bytes, not an option of its own (`curl -u u:$(curl -u u:pw …)` proposes nothing), a header whose credentials start inside the last one's credentials is their rest (`Authorization:${T}:Authorization:…` proposes nothing), and the computed check comes before a value's other checks, so the scan's work grows linearly with the prompt (`TestScanTimeShapes`, `BenchmarkScanShapes`: nested and unterminated substitutions, many options, options inside other words, deep quoting and braces, many headers, headers glued together, at 4 to 32 KiB; each 32 KiB one about 50 to 90 ms). Computed: every `$` it expands outside single quotes, in double quotes or none (a name, a digit, a special parameter `$$` `$?` `$@` `$*` `$!` `$#` `$-`, `${…}`, `$(…)`, `$((…))`, `$[…]`, an unquoted `$"…"`), a backquoted command, an escape inside `$'…'`; for curl also a byte of the rest of the password's word, and one before the password when its colon is inside it (`${C:-u:pw}`): `curl -u "u:abc$(cmd)"`, `curl -u "u:abc$$"`, `curl -u u:abc$(id)` and `curl --user u:abc$((1+2))` propose nothing (review T4, T4 (p2)); `\$HOME`, `'$HOME'`, `"ab$'c"`, `$'abc'` and a `$` before nothing it expands, `abc$`, `a$%b`, are typed. The tuning round's quoted words and named lines also refuse a template anywhere in the value (`${`, `$(`, `{{`; any other `$` is a password's byte there, `P@$$w0rd`: prose is no shell). A header credential refuses those too, and what the shell computes in it, by the same reader. In a curl command (its name in a word after a `curl` word of its command, before any quote left open), each credential byte is judged by the quotes of the word that holds the name, read from that word's start: `-H ""Authorization:'Bearer P@$$w0rd '`, `-H 'X-Token: -H Bearer P@$$w0rdP@$$w0rd '` (a `-H` inside the quotes), `-H 'X-<256 bytes>: Bearer …'` and `-d '{"Authorization": "Bearer P@$$w0rd"}'` propose `P@$$w0rd…`, while `-H ''Authorization:"Bearer $$'x"` and `-H "X-'Authorization: Bearer abc$HOME"` propose nothing (`TestScanHeaderQuoting`: 26 contexts, a literal and a `$$` value in each). Out of one (prose, a pasted request, JSON, a quote left open before the name: `With curl it's -H "…"`), from the argument's start as typed near the name: the quote right before the header's name (`"Authorization": "…"`, `$'…'`), else the argument of the last `-H` or `--header` before it on its line (prose's `-H 'X-Token: Bearer …'`), else the name, unquoted. Never the byte after the credential (`-H "Authorization: Bearer abc$TOKEN"` and `-H "Authorization: Bearer $$'suffix"` propose nothing, `-H 'Authorization: Bearer abc$HOME'` and `-H 'Authorization: Bearer P@$$w0rd '` propose `abc$HOME` and `P@$$w0rd`: review T4 (p2), T3P-1). So out of a curl command a header further into another quoted argument reads as unquoted (`echo 'see Authorization: Bearer abc$HOME'` proposes nothing). A value found is proposed again at its other exact occurrences on word boundaries (`repeat`, each its own candidate) when it has a digit or a symbol or 16 bytes. Never: templates and references (`${X}`, `$X`, `$(…)`, `{{ … }}`, `<…>`, `%X%`, `%(x)s`), calls and dotted names in code (`os.getenv("X")`, `process.env.X`, `response.access_token`), redactions (`***`, `•••`, `…`, `REDACTED`, `xxxx`), placeholders (`your…`, `…_here`, `replace…`), booleans and null, paths, a public SSH key, the bridge's own references (row 6). A weak password **is** a candidate when it is plainly the value assigned (`password=example`, prose that says the password was set to `` `example` ``): the review decides, not a list; a template, a redaction, a placeholder and a name without a value stay clean in every syntax, as does a header's `Bearer [token]`. |
| 5 | File bytes, per syntax | A file holds **exactly the source bytes of the approved range as typed**, for every syntax: no unescaping, no percent-decoding, no trimming, no added newline, no normalization. Double-quoted (JSON, shell, TOML, YAML): the bytes between the quotes, backslash escapes kept; single-quoted: the bytes between the quotes (YAML's doubled `''` kept, and a shell's `'\''`, which goes on with the word: `PASSWORD='abc'\''def'` gives `abc'\''def`, `encoded`); backticks and curly quotes in prose likewise; unquoted: to the next blank (or a `;Key=`, `&key=`, `,key=` that starts another pair), without trailing `.` `,` `;` `:` or an unbalanced closing bracket or quote: inside quotes punctuation stays. URL passwords and query values: percent-encoding kept. Header credentials (`Authorization`, a bare `Bearer`): to the next blank, quote or backslash, symbols kept (`Bearer AKIA…!…` is whole), without a sentence's trailing `.` `,` `;` `:` when a blank follows or the sentence ends there, but a header line's value keeps its line's bytes (`Authorization: Bearer abc!.:\r\n` gives `abc!.:`); `Basic`: the base64 as typed, not decoded. curl's `-u user:password`: after the first colon, the shell word as typed (quotes and escapes kept; a word that is one quoted string, `$'…'` too, without its quotes: `curl -u "user:pa\"ss"` gives `pa\"ss`, `encoded`), the word ending at an unquoted blank or operator, never inside a quote or substitution, and in a `$(…)` or backquotes at their close (row 4's reader). PEM: BEGIN to END line, line ends as typed (CRLF too). YAML block scalar: from its first content byte to the end of its last content line, the continuation lines' indentation kept. A YAML plain scalar with blanks is cut at its first blank (the review corrects it). A candidate whose bytes hold an escape, percent-encoding or a block's indentation is `encoded`, so the review can say "stored as typed". A manual mark or a corrected range is the selected bytes, exactly. Decided by the user (2026-10-18), as policy: a YAML block scalar's candidate keeps this content range, from its first line's content to the end of its last content line with the continuation lines' indentation, so the prompt keeps its YAML shape once the range is replaced; a DSN (`postgresql://app:<pw>@host/db`) proposes its password alone (`url-password`), not the connection string (the user widens it in the review); and a file always holds the raw typed bytes (`encoded`), never a decoded value. |
| 6 | Reference | `[secret in file <absolute path>]` in place of each protected range: plain words, the path whole (the directory may only hold `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -` and `/`, so the path is one word and never holds `]`), **never `@path`** (Claude Code reads an `@` mention into the conversation). Harness translation leaves it alone (`/name/more` is a path to it). **A scan never proposes the bridge's own references** (a sent prompt edited and sent again): exactly `[secret in file <path>]` where the path has the shape of its directory's files, `<directory>/<owner>/<file>` with both names as `secretfiles` makes them (`Files.IsFilePath`; no file is read). Only those bytes are left out, and at most one quote, bracket or comma beside one (with blanks): the detectors read the text as typed and again with each own reference masked as one word, overlaps are resolved on the whole ranges, then each candidate keeps its parts outside the references (without the blanks at the cut). The mask stands for a value's place, not its content, so with own references present a span that owes its match to one suppresses no other: one the masked text gave for its value's shape (Gitleaks' rules, a header credential without a scheme or a bare `Bearer` one, a prose value: a format, a length or a digit) that runs into a reference, and one found as typed that a reference's own bytes cut short (an edge inside one, or its end at one's `[`). It ranks after every other span, and a span it beats keeps the parts no winner has, as candidates of their own with its own kinds (row 3, `kept`). So does a structural value that runs into one when a match typed whole inside it wins, its own range clear of every reference: a complete token, a header's credential, a URL's password (`PASSWORD="Prefix-77-ghp_…![…]Tail"` proposes `Prefix-77-`, `ghp_…`, `!` and `Tail`; `PASSWORD="Bearer abcdefghij1234567890 […] tail"` proposes `Bearer`, the credential and `tail`; and, chosen, `PASSWORD="ghp_…,extra […]"` proposes `,extra`, which `token=ghp_…,extra` without a reference does not). Every other span keeps its rank, so a value's own boundary through a reference still wins (url-query `[…]` over prose `[…]&x=1`, and over `PASSWORD="https://h/x?token=[…]&x=1"`'s value: `&x=1` is never proposed). A value that runs into one is no code either: a dotted name glued to one is a value (`PASSWORD=[…]eyJ….eyJ….sig` proposes the rest). That is read from the own references' spans in the masked pass, never from the bytes a value holds (review T6: typed `response.Qz7Qz7`, the mask's spelling, was proposed with no reference at all). So a value next to one, on either side, quoted or not, is proposed whatever it holds (`PASSWORD="!@#%&+=?_- […]"` proposes `!@#%&+=?_-`, `password=[…]a` proposes `a`, `()[]{}` beside one is proposed), while `secret=([…])` proposes nothing and a sent prompt's text scans clean (a header credential protected out of a quoted value is the exception, as a token is: `PASSWORD="Bearer […] tail"` proposes `Bearer` and `tail` again, since the mask cannot vouch for the header); text that only looks like one (another path, a forged name) is scanned as any other text. A false candidate costs a review, a missed one a raw send. Review S1: any reference-shaped text, or a value holding the prefix, hid real candidates (`PASSWORD="Value-77! [secret in file /x]"`, a GitHub token inside a forged reference were sent without review); pass 2: a part with no letter or digit was dropped as punctuation, and an unquoted value read past a reference only up to the reference's first blank, so symbol-only passwords beside one, and anything glued after one, were sent raw; pass 3: the mask completed a token format (`ghp_` and 24 typed characters ran 12 bytes into a reference), that match beat the password's own, and only the token's head was proposed, so the password's rest was sent raw; pass 4: ranking it last was not enough, since the value's own span could be borrowed too (unquoted prose, a bare `Bearer`, a header without a scheme: shaped), and among borrowed spans the provider's format won again (`the password is ghp_…[…]Tail-Sentinel-77!` proposed `ghp_…` alone), so a borrowed winner now takes no bytes from the spans it beats (`TestScanReferenceMatrix`: token families, syntaxes, a reference before, after, inside, two, and letters, symbols or a wrapper after); the tuning round's pass: a complete token typed inside such a value was not borrowed, took the value's other bytes and sent its typed prefix raw (`PASSWORD="Prefix-Sentinel-77-ghp_…![…]Tail-Sentinel-77!"`), in every syntax, shaped containers too (unquoted prose, a bare `Bearer`), so a match typed whole inside a value that runs into a reference lends as a borrowed one does (the matrix's layouts with typed bytes before the token). |
| 7 | Storage | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/herdr-world/secrets/<owner>/<file>` (`--secrets-dir`, `HERDR_WORLD_SECRETS_DIR`; without the variable a validated `/run/user/<uid>`; no usable private runtime directory: the protection is unavailable and a review that protects anything is `secrets_unavailable`, never a send of the raw text and never a disk-backed fallback). Every operation walks from `/` one component at a time with `openat2(RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS\|RESOLVE_BENEATH)` (an `O_NOFOLLOW` component at a time on ENOSYS), directories above owned by root or us and not writable by others unless sticky, the directory itself ours and exactly 0700, made (with its parent, at most) when missing; owner directories 0700 and files 0600, checked on the descriptor, created exclusively, written whole, removed on any failure; an unsafe directory is refused, never repaired. Names from `crypto/rand.Text`. A lock file: one bridge holds a directory at a time (another is `available: false`). SQLite keeps only the owners (opaque directory, kind, worker id or pending token, created, expiry) and the file names: never a secret byte. Linux only; elsewhere `secretfiles.Open` is `ErrUnsupported` (the darwin helper still builds). |
| 8 | Owners and lifecycle | An owner is a **worker** (its id; files live until it really ends) or a **pending owner** (a random token with an expiry, for a route with no worker yet, rounds 2+: `Claim` gives its files to the worker it became; unclaimed, they go at the expiry). A worker's files go when it **really ends**: closed in herdr while its floor runs (`syncWorkers`' `CloseWorker`) or sent home (its removal and `finishFire`); **not** when its floor sleeps or its herdr session goes (it resumes), nor when the switch goes off. A janitor at start and every 5 minutes removes the files of a worker neither the hub nor the store has open (closed or unknown), expired pending owners', owner directories with no row and files with no row, and forgets rows whose files are gone; names it does not make are left alone. It reads which workers are open (the hub's, the store's) **with the files locked**, so no file is written or claimed between that read and the sweep: a worker whose files are there was open before them (review S2: read before the lock, a worker that started and wrote in between lost its file). A herdr close that was only transient releases the files as it ends a wrap-up. Round 5: a file another live worker holds by a lease outlives its owner, and a revoke removes a worker's files at once (rows 50–53). Unlinking is **not** a secure erasure (tmpfs pages can be swapped; an open descriptor keeps reading). |
| 9 | Revision | An HMAC-SHA256 with a random 32-byte key the bridge process keeps in memory, over the text, the rule set's version (`gitleaks-v8.30.1+structural-1`; `+entropy-1` since #163) and the candidates (ranges, kinds, `encoded`). Never a plain hash of the text (a short secret could be guessed offline from it). The key changes when the switch changes and at a restart: every review before is `secrets_review_stale`. |
| 10 | Checking a review | The bridge scans the submitted text again and checks the decisions against that scan, never the client's list: the revision is the scan's (else stale); exactly one decision per candidate; ranges (UTF-16 code units, `[start, end)`) non-empty, inside the text, never inside a surrogate pair (a combining mark may be split from its base: a code point boundary); protected ranges and **ignored candidates** apart from one another (a mark over an ignored occurrence is refused: an ignored occurrence stays exactly as typed, the user corrects the candidate instead). Anything else is `secrets_review_required`; errors name decisions by index and candidates by id, never text. `secrets_review_stale` and `secrets_review_required` both mean: scan again and review. |
| 11 | Order and limits | Scans and file writes never run on the hub goroutine: worker.prompt's on its worker's input lane (so it stays in order with the worker's other input), in one of 4 slots, 10 s each (past it `secrets_unavailable`, with no review: what the scan still writes is never read; a write that ends after its caller gave up removes its files). The files are written **first**, before translation, `/handoff`, storage, the audit and the send; then today's checks run on the text with its references: a prompt that fits as typed but not with its references is refused with the usual `bad_request` and its files are removed. With the switch on, a prompt over 32 KiB (`herdr.MaxPrompt`) is refused whole, never scanned in part. |
| 12 | Retry and failure | The identical submission (same worker, revision and decisions, in any order) within 5 minutes of a sent one reuses its files; a send that fails removes the files **it** made, never files it reused from one sent before (they belong to that sent prompt). A `/handoff <instruction>`'s files follow its request's prompt. Until the worker's input lane begins to send it, the request's end decides: a request refused at once or failing later (no handoff skill, the request over the limits with its references, its transcript not found, a person taking over, the worker gone, a cancel) and an `existing` answer (another request used none of the text) remove the files the submission made, never those it reused. From then on the send's result decides, whatever ended the request (and answered its command) meanwhile: sent, or failed without knowing whether any of it reached the terminal (herdr's submit or queue failed, typing stopped part-way, Enter not taken), the files stay the worker's and serve its retry; refused before any of it reached the terminal (the worker asking, blocked or not ready), they go. The removal runs off the hub goroutine (`agentAsk.settle`, `settleHandoff`; `agentHandoff.sending` hands the settle to the send, the prompt's errors from before the terminal are marked `unsent`). Review R1: the files stayed the worker's once the request started, whatever its end; review P2-1: a cancel or a takeover while the prompt was being submitted removed the files the delivered prompt refers to. A plain prompt's failed send still removes the files it made, whatever the failure (a typed prompt that failed part-way may leave references in the agent's input). |
| 13 | Audit and messages | `worker.prompt`'s audit row keeps the text's lengths and how many decisions protect and ignore; `prompt_secrets.scan`'s the text's lengths. A refusal never quotes the text; `PromptResult.sent` (to the sender only) shows the references, and ignored candidates as typed; a `/handoff`'s ack too, once its request is sent (the composer's text, with `protected`; review R2), never an `existing` answer's. |
| 14 | Telegram | A reply has no review: with the switch on and candidates found it is refused with a fixed sentence ("it may hold a password or another secret. Send it from the game…"), never its text, nothing typed. A clean reply goes as before. |
| 15 | What is NOT protected | The agent can still read a file with `cat` or a Read tool and print it into its transcript; other processes of the same Unix user can read it; text typed straight into a terminal, prompts sent before the switch was on and transcripts that already hold a secret are untouched; a secret the scan does not find is sent as typed unless the user marks it, and a paste into an agent's terminal can only be marked when the scan finds something in it (round 3 row 35: to mark a value the scan missed, send it from the P overlay or the laptop's prompt box instead); unlinking is not erasure. Later tool use is protected only once a credential-consuming route that never returns the bytes exists (a follow-up ticket, row 59). |

### Round 2: every other route

Round 1's gate (`protectText`) on every other route that takes typed text to an agent, a language model or storage;
code in `internal/server/promptsecretroutes.go` (fields, `startGated`, `queueReviewed`, the hand-over, stored records)
and each route's file; the protocol in `docs/protocol.md` "Prompt secrets" → "Round 2: every other route".

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | Several texts in one command | **A review per text**, keyed by its path in the args (`run.start` `text`, `extra`, `prompt`; `worker.answer_ask` `prompt`, `answers[N].other`; `worker.answer_followup` `note`, `answers[N].value`, `answers[N].note`; `worker.answer_async` `answers[N].answer`): `secrets` is then an object of reviews (`proto.SecretsReviews`), each of that text alone as sent, never of a prompt the bridge composes (the client does not hold it, and the bridge's own words would be scanned). Every text goes through the gate, so no protected value survives in another field: `run.start`'s ticket text is the composed prompt's, `run_launch.ticket_text` and the run's label are made from it with its references, the ack's `prompt` is the protected one. A review keyed by a text the command does not send (`extra` beside an edited `prompt`) is refused, as is a text with candidates and no review; the message names the path. Single-text commands keep round 1's `SecretsReview`. Rejected: one review over the composed prompt (`run.start` without `prompt`, the follow-up's answers: the client cannot address it), and a primary text with the others refused when they hold candidates (a ticket text with a password could not be started at all). |
| 17 | Owners of a command with no worker yet | A **pending owner** (30 minutes, `Options.SecretPendingTTL`). A hire's (`worker.hire`, `run.start`) is claimed by the new worker once herdr shows it (then the janitor counts it as the worker's), before its first prompt; a hire that fails removes it at once; a bridge stopped meanwhile leaves it to expire. Claiming at the minted id instead would need the janitor to know hires in flight; claiming after the send would leave a window where the agent reads expired files. A hire that succeeds keeps its files also when its prompt did not go (a resend refers to them). Each hire writes its own: a retried hire is refused by its taken desk as today and leaves none. `secretfiles.Claim` now refuses an expired owner and one already claimed (`ErrNotPending`). |
| 18 | Previews and their follow-up | `packup.detect` and `hire.interpret` gate their text before the model reads it and answer the text it read (`sent`; hire.interpret's `text`, `hire.sources`, `hire.task`) and an opaque **`secrets_pending`** hand-over: a random token, in memory only (a restart makes it unknown, its files expire), never the owner's directory name, bound to the reviewer (a switch change makes it stale), to packup's worker (a hire's has none), and to the texts the bridge answered as reviewed. The follow-up (`worker.prompt` after packup; the next `hire.interpret` and `worker.hire` after hire.interpret) sent with it needs **no review again for exactly those texts** (what the user left as typed is not proposed twice; references scan clean anyway, round 1 row 6), and claims its files: once only, for one worker. The claim comes **before** its text goes on, with the hand-over checked again then (expiry, the switch, its worker): `worker.prompt`'s on the worker's lane before the send, `worker.hire`'s once its worker is seen, before its prompt (fix round of review B1: a command can wait on the lane or on herdr past the hand-over's expiry, and must then send nothing rather than references to removed files). A send that fails after the claim leaves the files with the worker, for its retry; a claim after the send (round 2's first cut) could ack a prompt whose files were gone. A text that differs is reviewed as any. Without the hand-over, a pending proposal's sentences must have no candidate (a client's own sentence, or one from before the switch, is never read raw). A dictation's later sentences join the same owner and token. Rejected: re-reviewing follow-ups (two dialogs for one prompt) and accepting any substring of a reviewed text (any text can be spelled from a long one). |
| 19 | Stored prompts | A schedule's or a hire preset's prompt keeps **no protected file** (files outlive no agent: they are bound to a run). With the switch on, every create and update scans it: candidates need a review whose decisions all **ignore**; one that protects anything is `secrets_review_stored` (a new code: "remove the value, or protect it when you hire"). An update that only moves the due time is reviewed too: always reviewing keeps every stored record current, and a client that saves without one gets the error rather than a schedule whose fire will fail. The row keeps a **record**: `promptsecret.StoredDigest`, a plain SHA-256 of the rule set, the text and its candidates (the prompt is stored in plain beside it; a revision is keyed and dies with the process, a record must survive restarts). `hire_preset.check` takes the same review before the classifier reads the prompt. A preset's prompt reaches an agent only through `worker.hire`, reviewed there. Off, nothing is scanned and an update leaves the record alone: it matches only the text it was made of. |
| 20 | A schedule's fire | Fires, `schedule.retry` and `schedule.run_now` with the switch on scan the stored prompt in `runHire` before anything reaches herdr (off the hub goroutine, after the desk and name are held): no candidates, or the record of a review that left them as typed, and it fires as before; otherwise the hire fails through its usual path, so the schedule is `failed` with a reason that says to open and review it (the `schedule.upsert` is the notice: schedules have no other), never a raw send. Off, as before. **The way out (fix round, review B4):** `schedule.retry` (and `schedule.run_now`) take an optional `secrets`, the review of the stored prompt, checked as a save's (all ignore, else `secrets_review_stored`); its record is saved on the row, then the schedule fires as typed. Chosen over letting `schedule.update` act on a `failed` schedule: retry is #62's existing way out of `failed`, so the state machine is unchanged (no `failed` → `scheduled` edge, no new due time to pick), and the prompt the user reviews is exactly the one stored. Round 2's first cut told the user to open, review and save, which a failed schedule refuses: only switching the feature off recovered it. |
| 21 | Limits | Each route checks its text as typed first (no file for a text that never fits), then again with its references (the route's own checks run on the protected text: `hireShape`, `ValidMessage`, `checkTyped`, `hireintent.ValidText`'s 8 KiB, `agentInstruction`'s 4 KiB, the wrap-up's room, `maxAsyncAnswer`, `maxRunText`), removing its files on failure. |

A model call (previews, `hire_preset.check`, an LLM handoff) waits for one of the AI service's 2 slots: `ai.WithGate` carries the check in its ctx, and the service asks it once the call holds a slot (the fakes before they record a call), so each call is refused, nothing sent, if the review went stale while it waited; a preview or preset check whose review went stale by the time its model answered answers `secrets_review_stale` (a preview's files go: its hand-over could not be used). Once the first byte of a text went, nothing is checked again (Enter retries, a retried model request, a steer's fallback turn). `run.start`'s work-item continuation checks it too (nothing hired). A schedule's fire is exempt: its stored record does not depend on the reviewer. A switch turned on while an unreviewed command waits changes nothing, as in round 1.
