| 12 | Measured | Isolated harness (`browser.mjs`, headless Chromium 149, no scene) on the worst Claude page (1,070 items): first frame **2,006 ms → 42 ms** after `setItems`, longest task 1,298 ms → none over 50 ms, 43,272 → 4,206 elements, every row built 234–253 ms after `setItems`; over 64 pages (warm) the first frame's median 517 → 41 ms. After review round 2 (every diff line drawn): first frame 34–38 ms, every row built ~105 ms and the last of its 9,320 diff lines in at 359–367 ms after `setItems` (40,686 elements), no frame over 17 ms from the first frame to the last line; over 64 pages (warm) the first frame's median 29 ms, max 38 ms. In the app (`app.mjs`: the Vite dev server, demo-m5 with the scene, the same page as the sat-at worker's transcript, headless): sit to first painted rows **3.6–4.5 s → 0.36–0.43 s**, longest frame gap **3.4–4.3 s → 100 ms** (200 ms once; the scene alone: 17 ms). Round 2: first rows 284–344 ms, every row 632–708 ms, the last diff line 956–1,027 ms; no frame over 50 ms while the diffs are drawn; the longest frame while rows fill in 66–91 ms, as before the fix (77–83 ms: a `ResizeObserver` callback's forced layout during the backfill, no script over 50 ms). Numbers: docs/research/transcript-open.md, "Implementation results". |
| 13 | Tests | `transcriptOpen.dom.test.ts` (fake timers): opening vs empty, a resync that keeps its rows, the newest rows first and slices in order, a slice's budget, the place held and the bottom followed, an image run merged across a slice boundary with no slice looking at the whole timeline, a resync and a destroy during the backfill, live updates during it, a jump to a row not built, system rows built when shown with counts kept, tool counts from the items, a diff's lines drawn near the view with #21's default and its counts, "Show next" before drawing; round 2: every diff line drawn once the open settles with no observer ever firing (at the top, in the middle, in backfilled rows, in the newest; a page with no backfill; "Show next" and its state across a new row; a resync and a live update during the drawing; going away; "Hide tool calls" on; "Show changes" off then on; a body not reported away left to the observer; a drained one that comes near; End during the drawing; the per-frame cap), and the loader under "Hide tool calls" (the first build out of time on hidden rows, the slice that builds the first row that shows, only rows that show and an image run once counted, a page where nothing shows, the pref and "Show system" changed meanwhile). `find.mjs` (headless Chromium): `window.find` from the bottom and the loader at 4x CPU slowdown on synthetic pages. `transcriptMode.test.ts`: the host's `loading` until the ack, the `frame` deferral, the stand-in, a child's. `transcript.integration.test.ts`: a child's outline then its pending words; updated for system rows built when shown. |

## 2026-10-20 — #126 (bridge): a big line's list item without its base64, and each watch's read cost logged

The first page of a 220 MB Codex rollout took ~1.9 s to read after a ~1.3 s index build: `Log.items` read every line of
the page back and parsed it in full. Its big lines are not tool text: they are inline images (`input_image` data URLs in
`custom_tool_call_output` and user messages, `item_completed` Extension events repeating a generated image's base64),
and so are all 732 local lines of 256 kB and more (565 MB, of which 1.7 MB is not base64). Code:
`internal/transcript/biglines.go`, `Log.scan` / `Line` / `readLine` (`log.go`), `inspectInline` (`images.go`),
`logTranscriptRead` (`internal/server/transcript.go`). Investigation: docs/research/transcript-open.md.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What a list item skips | A line of at least **256 kB** (`bigLine`) gets a record when it is indexed: the runs to skip of its JSON string values (never keys) that are base64 (an optional `data:…;base64,` header, then only `A–Z a–z 0–9 + / = - _`, no escape) and at least **128 kB** long (`minCut`), and its inline images' refs. A capped read (a page, a push, `Images`) reads the line around those runs and parses that. `full` reads (`transcript.item`, an image's bytes) read the whole line as before. |
| 2 | Why the list item cannot change | A cut keeps the string's first `max(MaxText, MaxDiffBytes)+1` bytes (`cutKeep`): more than any capped field shows of one string (a text part, an output, a notice, a diff line within its budget, a 4 kB input dropped either way), and long enough that every cap still sees it was longer and sets the same `truncated` flags. A base64 string has no newline, quote, escape or marker, so a cap, a first-line summary or a prefix check reads nothing past that prefix. So base64 printed as text (a tool's output) is capped exactly as before, and a parser branching on an empty string sees a non-empty one. A cut image's base64 is only a prefix, so its ref comes from the record (`imgSrc.known`). Checked: every item of all 432 local transcripts of 1 MB and more (264,018 items, 676 records), built both ways, byte for byte equal (a one-off run, not committed); the tests below on synthetic big lines and on every fixture made big. |
| 3 | Per line, not per item | A record is per line, so an item's grouping (a call and its result, merges, interruptions) is untouched and nothing is rebuilt when an item gains a line. It holds offsets and a few image facts, never a parse (the parsers' closures hold whole raw values, Claude's `toolUseResult` among them) and never bytes: the index still holds no transcript. Records are made off the lock and never changed once in the index; a capped parse whose inline images are not the record's (the file changed) reads the whole line instead. |
| 4 | Images hashed when indexed | A list item's image refs carry the hash, mime, bytes and size, so a big line's inline images are decoded and hashed when the line is indexed (the build, a tail's line, a `Read` log's `Refresh`), not when an item is built: the bytes are not kept and not put in the image cache. In the build that runs beside the scan, within 32 MiB of lines at a time (`resolving`), and the build is ready once they are done. At page time such an image registers its place (`hashLoc`, `Knows`) as before, so only items that were shown make an image fetchable; its first fetch reads its line again (`Image`) and caches the bytes then. A big line that a list never shows is hashed anyway: the build's cost follows the file's image bytes, not the page's. |
| 5 | Measured (`open.go`, `Follow` → `Ready` → `Subscribe(200)`, three passes, this host, interleaved) | Codex 220 MB: build 1.28–1.30 → 1.62 s, first page **1.87–2.00 s → 34–37 ms** (build + page 3.2 → 1.7 s). Codex 17 MB: build 103–106 → 133–162 ms, page 140–146 → 6 ms. Codex 6.9 MB: 53–56 → 72–74 ms, 72 → 18–20 ms. Claude 29.5 MB: 148–153 → 182–186 ms, 183–186 → 64–66 ms. Claude 24.8 MB: 139–140 → 164–174 ms, 110–111 → 36–38 ms. Page JSON unchanged. The build's added cost is the hashing it now does (beside the scan) and the base64 scan (8 bytes at a time, `b64Word`). Under `-race` the instrumented hashing and scan cost more: a 12.7 MB image line builds in 2.1 s instead of 1.5 s (its page 8 ms instead of 1.7 s), and a watch whose page leaves such a line out (`TestTranscriptImages`, limit 1) now pays it in the build; that test and `TestLogoSVGDrawnByWorker` time out in a full `-race` run of `internal/server` on the base commit too. |
| 6 | Not done here | A big line that is escaped text (a multi-MB output with newlines) is still read whole: none exists locally (the largest non-base64 big line is 288 kB). Hidden items still come along and count nothing toward a page: that waits on the client's result (#126 parts 1 and 2). |
| 7 | Each watch's cost | Debug, like the hub's other per-watch lines: **`transcript watch read`** with `client`, `worker`, `child`, `req_id`, `wait_ms` (from the offer of a log to its `Ready`: the build, 0 when the log was built already), `page_ms` (`Subscribe`), `items`, `limit` and `bytes`: the ack's encoded size, or for a watch that was pending, the size of the push that carried its first page (`req_id` empty). Sizes and times only. The ack is now encoded on the watch's goroutine (`replyAck`), so its size is known and a large ack is no longer encoded on the hub goroutine; `transcript watch acked empty` is unchanged. |
| 8 | Tests | `internal/transcript` (`biglines_test.go`): `TestB64Cuts` (values, keys never cut, data URLs, too short, escapes, text around, after escaped quotes, unterminated); `TestB64Word` (every byte value in every place of a word, against the table); `TestCappedBigLines` (Claude: a user image, a Read's image with its `toolUseResult` copy, base64 printed as text, big escaped text, a Write of base64 content, a mixed result, a hidden attachment; Codex: a user image, a tool output of two data URLs, an Extension `item_completed` and its `image_generation_end`, base64 and escaped outputs, a patch adding a base64 file: every item equal to the whole-line build, images hashed, outputs truncated, and `Item` still untruncated); `TestCappedFixtures` (every fixture, each line given a big base64 field no parser reads); `TestCappedPageSkipsBase64` (a page reads no cut byte, the image's bytes still fetch); `TestCappedMismatchReadsWholeLine`; `TestCappedLiveLines` (lines a tail adds). `internal/server`: `TestTranscriptReadLog` (the ack's fields and size, a pending watch's first push, no transcript text in the log). |

## 2026-10-20 — #142: world events are not interaction (idle stays at 60 Hz)

With a live bridge the game targeted 120 Hz most of the idle time: every world event (`applyChange`), every board push
(`pushBoards`), a whiteboard render loading and a merge gong reset the 1.5 s activity window. Code: `App.tick`,
`render/framePolicy.ts`.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What counts as activity | Input, camera moves and scene transitions (`activity`), and while they run: walking, a camera tween, the doors, arrivals, busy boards (`tick`'s active test). A world event, a board push, a whiteboard render arriving or a gong ring is not: idle draws it on its next frame (60 Hz; 30 with battery saver). The gong's swing and the merge fly-offs ask for frames through `boardsBusy`, from the next frame on. No new pacing path. |
| 2 | Policy | Unchanged: decision row 3 (2026-09-28): 120 Hz interacting, 30–60 Hz idle, paused when hidden. |
| 3 | Measured | `__h3d.pacing()` counts `tick`'s decisions per display frame (headless Chromium draws 60 Hz either way). demo-m5 / demo-m6 with `sim=1&simusage=250` (~64 world events/s), 5 s with no input after 2.5 s: before, every decision was the fast rate (city 197/197, `lab` with board polls 198/198, battery saver 194/194 at 60); after, none (217/217 at 60, 216/216, 213/213 at 30). Test: `e2e/h142-idle-pacing.spec.ts`, with a wheel as the positive control (fast rate within the window, idle after). |

## 2026-10-20 — #134: the hire and start-run dialogs open on a preview of the local refs, not a fetch

`hire.prepare` and `run.prepare` ran `git fetch origin` on every call, so Hire, Hire Review and Start a run waited for
origin before they showed their options; Start a run fetched again on every pause in typing (its prompt preview is a
`run.prepare`). A slow or unreachable origin held a dialog up to the fetch's 20 s timeout, even for a hire or run without
a worktree, and the worktree hire then fetched again anyway before choosing its base.

| # | Decision | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | One capability for both prepares | The snapshot's `prepare_preview: true`; `hire.prepare` and `run.prepare` take `preview: true` and then read the repository root, the default branch and the local `origin/<default>` commit without fetching. Everything else (choice, name, capacity and host load, ticket and prompt) is prepared as before. `WorldStore.preparePreview` is reset on every snapshot, so an older bridge is never sent the field (it refuses unknown fields). |
| 2 | Where the game previews | Opening Hire, Hire Review, Start a run and a schedule's form; a folder change (Hire, Hire Review, the schedule form); every debounced field change of Start a run; Try again after a failed open. The schedule form never fetches: its hire fetches when it fires, so origin now says nothing about then. |
| 3 | Where it still fetches | The bridge: `beginHire`, shared by `worker.hire`, `run.start` and a schedule's fire, fetches before it chooses a worktree's base and refuses a failed fetch (`fetch_failed`), unchanged. The game: Fetch again, and the recheck after a `capacity` or `fetch_failed` refusal (Hire, Start a run, and new in Hire Review, which had none: a review opened on a preview would otherwise keep a worktree it cannot make). Start a run keeps asking for a fetch until one answers (`fetchWanted`), so a field typed while Fetch again is on its way does not turn it into a preview. |
| 4 | A preview does not hide a fetch | A dialog keeps a fetch's answer over a later preview of the same repository (`newerGit`): typing in Start a run after a fetch refusal keeps the failure, its Fetch again and the worktree off. Nor does a preview cancel a fetch still on its way: in Hire and Hire Review a Folder changed while the recheck after a refusal is out (a preview, so the folder answers at once) leaves the recheck's answer adopted when it comes, as long as the form still shows that repository and no newer fetch was sent (`OriginFetches`, beside `newerGit`); another repository's folder is a fresh start. Hire Review checks a typed folder on leaving the field too: that answer may draw the field again under the typing, and the new field sends no `change`. Start a run has no Folder: an edit while a fetch is wanted fetches itself (`fetchWanted`). The schedule form never fetches (its hire fetches when it fires). |
| 5 | Honest wording | `git.preview: true`, `fetched: false`, no `fetch_error`: nothing was checked, so nothing failed, and the worktree stays on offer (`worktreeUsable`, `fetchNote`). The base line says what it is: "A new h3d/… branch from `origin/main @ 1a2b3c4, 3 h old` (last fetched; refreshed before branching)"; without local origin refs, "`origin/HEAD` (not fetched into this checkout yet; checked before branching)". The wait no longer says "and origin" where the bridge previews. |
| 6 | The simulator previews too | `fixture-sim` advertises `prepare_preview` and takes `preview` on both prepares; `e2e/m4.spec.ts`'s failed-fetch test now reaches the failure through the refused worktree hire and its recheck. The older-bridge path is covered by the DOM tests. |
| 7 | Measured | `go test ./internal/server -run TestPreparePreviewDoesNotWaitForFetch -v`: real WebSocket requests to a bridge whose fake fetch takes 250 ms. Without `preview` (today's behaviour): `hire.prepare` 250.5 ms, `run.prepare` 250.8 ms. With it: first open, repeated open and an edit each 0.26–0.38 ms, no fetch. Isolated server timings, not the browser's. |
| 8 | Not done here | `run.prepare` with a board card that is not on the fetched board (`work_item`) still reads it from the tracker before answering (`workItemTicket`, bounded by `titleTimeout`); a blank open, a typed issue number or text never does. Host load reads `/proc`. |
| 9 | Tests | `internal/server` (`prepare_preview_test.go`): `TestPreparePreviewDoesNotWaitForFetch` (both commands: first and repeated open and an edit, no fetch; without `preview`, one fetch); `TestPreviewThenWorktreeStillFetches` (after previews of an offline origin, a worktree `worker.hire` and `run.start` are refused with `fetch_failed` and make nothing; online, both fetch and branch from `origin/main`). Game: `world/hire.test.ts` (labels, missing refs, `newerGit`), `world/store.test.ts` (reset), DOM tests of Hire, Hire Review (the new recheck), Start a run (`startRun.preview.dom.test.ts`: capability on and off, open and edits, the recheck, Fetch again, a field typed during Fetch again) and the schedule form; the simulator's; `e2e/m4.spec.ts`. The `children-*` fixtures change only by the flag. |

## 2026-10-20 — #143: the scene under the overview page draws at a few frames a second

The floor and all-floors overview pages are long-lived, opaque, full-viewport screens (`.ov`, `inset: 0`, `--ov-ink`),
and the scene behind them drew at the full idle rate (60 Hz, 120 with a walker or a busy board). Code:
`render/framePolicy.ts` (`Coverage`, `OPAQUE_HZ`, `SCRIM_HZ`), `OverviewOverlay.covering` (`ui/overview.ts`),
`App.tick` (`app.ts`). It extends 2026-09-28's frame-rate policy (row 3): nothing else of it changes.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The input | `FrameInputs.covered`: **`'none'`** (the default: every caller and rate as before), **`'scrim'`**, **`'opaque'`**. `targetHz` caps its result with it: hidden is still 0, battery saver and activity still pick the rate under the cap, and **the cap wins over activity** (a walker arriving, a busy board, a tween). |
| 2 | The opaque cap | **4 Hz** (`OPAQUE_HZ`). The scene cannot be seen, so only `step()` matters: the page's refresh (`stepOverview`, at most every 250 ms), the wall screen, the departures, the rack and the laptop watches tick there. With `shouldRender`'s quarter-frame slack that is a frame every 200 ms on a 60 Hz display (5/s) and every ~192 ms on a 120 Hz one (5.2/s): a status change reaches the page within the 250 ms gate plus one covered frame (≤ 450 ms). 3 Hz would land the ticks on the 250 ms gate itself, where vsync jitter makes every other refresh miss by a frame. Not 0 Hz: the page needs `step()`, and the e2e `frames()` waits (30 s) keep working with the page open. |
| 3 | The scrim cap | **20 Hz** (`SCRIM_HZ`) under the whiteboard (`WhiteboardOverlay.isOpen`, from its open to its finish): its 88–92 % scrim (`--scrim-board`) leaves the scene faintly visible, where motion barely reads, so it keeps moving rather than freezing; a third of the idle rate, a sixth of the active one (20/s on a 60 Hz display, 24/s on 120 Hz). |
| 4 | When the page counts | `OverviewOverlay.covering`: true once the **opening grow has played to its end** (the 420 ms clip-path grow, or the 140 ms calm fade; at once without Web Animations), across `a` (a switch in place, no grow), false **the moment a close starts** (`close()`, before the shrink), in `closeNow()` (a row's go-to) and at `finish()`. A grow cancelled by an Esc during it never counts. While either grow plays the scene draws at the normal rate: the clip path shows it. The page wins over the whiteboard. A seated transcript, the dialogs and every other surface cover part of the view only and keep today's rates. |
| 5 | Resuming | `tick` remembers the last coverage; when it drops (opaque → anything, scrim → none) it counts as activity (`activity(false)`): the rate is back to 120 Hz (60 with battery saver) at once, so the first vsync after the close starts draws, however recent the last covered frame, and the full rate holds for the active window while the page shrinks away. What that frame shows is current: everything it draws is stepped at it, and the world's poses are wall-clock (below). |
| 6 | `dt` under the page | `dt` stays capped at 0.1 s, so a `dt` integrator runs at ~40 % speed under the page; none of them is seen there and each goes on at full speed after: the daylight ease (`DaylightEase.step`, a 3 s ease toward the minute's light, a fraction of a degree of sun), the fire, mezzanine and lobby doors (`animateDoors`, `LobbyView.update`: eases toward open or shut, at most a door mid-swing on the frame back), the walker (`Walker.step`: the page stops and releases it and takes the keys, so only its eye and seat eases run, settled), the receptionist (`Reception.update`, its own clock clamped to 0.1 s: a line's mouthing and wave run longer in wall time, its bubble is timed apart) and the city camera's damping (`controls.update()`, per call: no input reaches it). The arrivals, `office.frame` / `city.frame`, the laptops, the tween, the overview wall, the departures and the rack all read the wall clock. |
| 7 | `rendered` | `App.rendered` (a worker's status as of the last frame drawn, `__h3d.status`) lags up to a covered frame under the page. Its readers are e2e polls with ≥ 10 s timeouts that read the status only; nothing reads its `at`. Left as it is. |
| 8 | Measured | This host (Chromium 149 headless, WebGL2 via ANGLE/Vulkan on an RTX 2060, Vite dev, load ~15–20), the page open and grown, 5 s windows, `Performance.getMetrics` deltas, base and after interleaved in one page (base: `covering` forced false), mean of 4 each: **perf-city240** 56.5 → **5.0** frames/s, TaskDuration 3.86 → **3.21** s/5 s (script 1.01 → 0.10); **perf-floor60** 58.4 → **5.0**, 2.95 → **1.21** s/5 s (script 1.66 → 0.12); **perf-floor96** 55.7 → **5.0**, 3.40 → **2.25** s/5 s (script 1.39 → 0.16). What is left on city240 is the page's own style work (RecalcStyle ~1.4 s/5 s, its lamp glows: #145), plus the GPU work saved, not measured here. |
| 9 | Tests | `framePolicy.test.ts` (the caps over active, battery and hidden; `'none'` unchanged; the rate the cap renders at on 60 and 120 Hz displays); `overview.dom.test.ts` (`covering`: after the grow, across a switch, off before the shrink, a cancelled grow, `closeNow`, no Web Animations); `e2e/h143-overview-pause.spec.ts` on demo-m118 with the simulator (the rate under the grown page, a status change reaching its row under it, the first frame after each close (the close button, Esc, a row's go-to) stepped to its own clock (`__h3d.frameAt` later than the last covered frame's) and showing a status injected just before the close, at the full rate, which holds during the shrink, the whiteboard's scrim rate). |

## 2026-10-20 — #132: a Codex poll of a background terminal names the command it waits on

A Codex `exec_command` still running when its wait ends leaves a session the model follows with `write_stdin` (a poll
when `chars` is empty). In code mode such a poll's row showed its raw script line (`const r = await
tools.write_stdin({session_id:84659,…})`). Code: `internal/transcript/polls.go`, `Log.terminals` / `Log.started` /
`items` (`log.go`), the call and result branches of `codexResponse` (`codex.go`), `CodexTerminals`, `Starts`,
`ReadChunk` / `Chunks` (`internal/activity/rules.go`). Real shapes: a catalogue of all 564 local rollouts (codex-cli
0.160.1–0.163.0), counts only.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is a poll row | A code-mode `exec` script whose only tool calls are `write_stdin`, or `write_stdin` and `view_image` (its image strip stays), and a direct `write_stdin`. A script that also runs an `exec_command` (or any other tool) keeps its own summary. Several polls in one script: the first one's command and `(+N more)`. |
| 2 | Where the session → command link lives | **In the index, built in file order** (`Log.index`, under `mu`, from `scan` and `Line` alike, on the full parse): an open call whose commands may start sessions waits in `Log.starting` (by entry; dropped at its result or an interruption); its result's output says which sessions started (`activity.Starts`) and their commands, first line clipped, go in `Log.sessions` (the newest 256, oldest dropped first); a poll's entry gets its session's command in `Log.polled` when it is indexed (one string per poll row of a known session, shared with the session map's). `items` hands it to the builder before the contributions apply. The parser stays stateless: a poll's process, wall time and new output come from its own result line. So a build from the file, a tail's lines and a `Read` (a subagent's transcript) give the same rows, and a capped list item the full one's summary (the summary never reads the line's big strings). Not in the parser (it has no state), not on every entry (the index lives as long as the watch). |
| 3 | Reusing the desk's parsing | One parser for both: `activity.Starts` is `Sessions.Started`'s matching, exported, and `Started` now calls it; the desk's `Nested` gains `Command` and `Chars`, set only by the new `CodexTerminals` (read without the shell rules), so `Sessions.put` (which drops a Kind-less entry) and `Resolve` are unchanged. **The chunk scan is now JSON-aware** (`ReadChunk`, a line at a time): `chunkRe`'s `[^{}]*` missed every chunk whose output holds a brace, chunks also come inside `Promise.allSettled`'s `{status, value}` / `{i, result}` and after Codex's "Warning: truncated output" note, and the positional match then failed: simulated on the rollouts, the old matching linked 66% of the polls whose session is a literal. The desk's poll labels gain the same (the #98 tests pass unchanged). Not done: reordering wrapped chunks by their `i`, matching several commands when the counts differ. |
| 4 | The summary | `Waited for <command>`; non-empty `chars`: `Sent <chars> to <command>`, the typed text scrubbed (`activity.Scrub`) then clipped to 40 runes, newline and return as `⏎`, other control characters as `^C`, `^D`, `^[`, `^?`. Then `(+N more)`; the command gives way to the 200-rune cap, `(+N more)` does not. Like Codex's own TUI ("Waited for background terminal"). **The process is not in the summary** (round 2): appended to it, the game's ellipsis cut it with the command, all of it at 390 px. It is the tool's own field, `terminal: {state: "running" \| "exited", exit_code?, wall_seconds?}` (wall: the poll's `wall_time_seconds`, else the direct header's `Wall time`, only while running), and the game words it (row 10). |
| 5 | Status and body | Exited with a non-zero code: `error`, as other failed tools. **Several polls in one script** (round 2): every chunk is read; the row's process is the first that exited other than 0, else the first chunk's that says one (a chunk that says neither is skipped), so one failed poll among several makes the row an error and shows its code. Chunks are not matched to the polls by position (a poll that prints `r.output` adds lines, not chunks). Still running: `ok` (the poll is done). No result yet: running, bare summary. The body (`output_text`) is the decoded output of the script's chunks (other lines, a truncation note among them, kept) or the text after a direct result's `Output:`; output that has no chunk (`text(r.output)`, 33 scripts, or none printed, 84) stays as it was, with no outcome. A chunk Codex cut (a fixture's) still gives its fields and its whole output, with "…". The raw script stays the row's `input`. |
| 6 | Where the start is missing | `background terminal <id>`, never the script: inherited history of a subagent rollout (hidden notices, never calls), a result without its call, a start whose output was cut or names no session, a session the map forgot, a session id in a variable (34 sites: `-1`, never 0, so it never passes for a command; the row says `background terminal`). A start whose command could not be read (a template literal `cmd`) names nothing. A session id reused later is keyed on its latest start. |
| 7 | Direct calls | No local rollout has a direct `exec_command` or `write_stdin`; their output (`Chunk ID: … Wall time: N seconds / Process running with session ID N` or `Process exited with code N … Output:`) is codex-rs's own strings: `polls_direct.jsonl` is synthetic and unverified. |
| 8 | Out of scope | Collapsing consecutive polls of one session into one row (the issue's item 4), and `cmd` as a template literal in `execSummary`. |
| 9 | Tests | `internal/activity`: `TestCodexTerminals` (bare and quoted keys, no chars, Ctrl-C both spellings, a template literal, a variable session, poll + image, poll + command, commands, poll + patch, direct calls; typed or run text: typed code, a grep for a call, escaped quotes, a template, a call in a `${…}` or a comment counts, a regex or a `${…}` in the object: every match counts, polls between regexes with quotes), `TestScriptCallsMatrix` (26 hazards: regexes with quotes, a class, escaped slashes, divisions, comments and templates with quotes, typed and run text holding calls; a real `write_stdin`, `exec_command` or `view_image` before, after and between every pair: 2,184 scripts), `TestClassifyRealToolCalls` (the desk: typed code is a poll, a grep for a call a command, a command between regexes), `TestStarts` (direct, chunks in order, braces, wrappers, a truncation note, the one-command fallback), the #98 test unchanged. `internal/transcript` (`polls_test.go`): `TestCodexPolls` (`polls.jsonl`, `polls_direct.jsonl`: running, exited 0 and 1, Ctrl-C, typed text, unknown, two polls, poll + image, poll + command, wrapped starts with braces, a truncation note, a variable session, `text(r.output)`, still waiting, across turns; direct ones), `TestCodexPollFallbacks` (a start with no session, a result without its call, eviction both ways, a subagent's inherited start), `TestPollSummary`, `TestPollOutput` (several polls: running + exited 0, exited 0 + 1, exited 1 + running, two failures, a poll with no chunk), `TestPollTypedCode`, `TestPollBetweenRegexes`, `TestPollsLiveAndCapped` (`Line` vs `scan`, a big poll + image line capped vs full); `TestExecSummary` updated. Game: `transcriptRender.test.ts` (#132: summaries, the process tag running / exited 0 / non-zero / none, the wait as the duration, the error row, the body, the strip), `fixture-transcript.test.ts` (`demo-h132`), `e2e/h132-codex-polls.spec.ts` (at 390 × 844 the tag whole inside its row and every clipping box, the command cut, Quiet and Ubuntu, light and dark). See it: `?ws=%2Ffixture%2Fdemo-h171%3Fsim%3D1%26simtx%3Ddemo-h132`, sit at Nibble on herdr-3d. |
| 10 | The process in the game | A tag right after the command (`.tx-tool-term`, `flex: none`: the command gives way, the tag never), outlined, in the summary's mono: `process running` (never the call's own `running`: the row's chip says the poll is `done`) or `exited N`, a non-zero exit in the error's red; the title says it in full (`The process is still running (the poll waited 30s)`, `The process exited with code 130`). The wait is the row's duration when the view did not see the call finish (history), as `duration()` formats it. Under a 520 px transcript the tag moves to a second line under the command, lined up with the tool's name: on one line at 390 px it left the command `Waite…`. The image strip's label keeps the summary alone; "Hide tool calls" and find in page are unchanged (the tag is text in the row). |
| 11 | Calls written inside strings | (round 3) `scriptCalls`, the desk's and the poll rows' one scanner, leaves out a `tools.<name>(` only when it is written inside **what a `write_stdin` types (`chars`) or what an `exec_command` runs (`cmd`)**: typed code (`chars: "await tools.exec_command(…)"`) is a poll, a `grep` for a call is a command. That value is found from the kept call's `({`, one `key: value` pair at a time (bare or quoted keys, shorthand, a string, a template without `${…}`, a number or a name; a backslash skips a byte; the value must be followed by `,` or `}`). Anything else in the object (an expression, a regex, a nested object, a newline in a quoted string, a `${…}`) and nothing in that call is text. Every other match counts, wherever it is (a comment, another string, a template's text), as before round 2: the script is not lexed, so a quote in a regex literal or a division can never hide a real call (round 2's lexer read `/"/ … /"/` as a string and dropped the poll between them). On the 11,696 real exec scripts: 7 lose 20 matches, all inside `chars` / `cmd` values; none lose one anywhere else. The one shape left: a fake call in text (a comment) whose fake `cmd` string closes inside real code, on one line, before a `,` or `}`. |

## 2026-10-20 — #145: the overview page's own cost: a lamp blink drawn once, rows off the view skipped, no rebuild on open

With the page open over a busy floor its own CSS cost more than the rest of the page: every working lamp animated its
`box-shadow` (a paint per lamp per frame, rows off the view included), every row ran its endless animation, and an open
rebuilt every row and laid the whole page out inside the key that opened it. Code: `game/src/ui/overview.css` (the
working lamp, `.ov-row`), `game/src/ui/overview.ts` (`show`, `reuse`, `focusSoon`, `finish`, `foldAway`); tests
`e2e/h145-overview-rows.spec.ts`, the opt-in `e2e/h145-overview-perf.spec.ts` (`H3D_PERF=1`) on `e2e/perfTrace.ts` (m58's
trace method), `tools/mac-runner.mjs` (`overview` jobs).

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The blink | The working lamp's body is drawn at 32 % (`color-mix` with transparent: the same as opacity 0.32 over any row) and over it, on its `::before`, the lit lamp with its halo and glow, drawn once; only that layer's `opacity` animates (`ov-blink`: 1 → 0 → 1, `--ov-blink`, ease-in-out). The body reads 1 → 0.32 → 1 exactly as before and the glow goes out with it; at the peak and the trough it is the old lamp to the pixel, in between the glow fades where it used to shrink. One animation and one layer per lamp, not two. Calm: the lit layer steady and without its glow (as before: the glow was only in the keyframes). |
| 2 | What else runs | The needs-you ring (`ov-ring`, opacity and transform) and the busy mark's leaves (`ov-busy-leaf`, transform) already were compositor motion; the flaps' skeleton (JS, `FlapClock`) runs only while a line waits for its first summary, writing a few attributes per frame (on a skipped row they cost no style, layout or paint); the 20 s since refresh rewrites changed times only. Blink still runs one main-thread style recalc per frame while any animation runs, composited or not, so the recalc count stays at the frame rate: what dropped is what each costs (the animated elements of the drawn rows only) and the paints (none). |
| 3 | Rows off the view | `.ov-row` is `content-visibility: auto` with `contain-intrinsic-block-size: auto` and a content-box estimate per kind, layout and theme (their padding and rule come on top), each the mean measured on perf-city240's every-floor page (All: 240 workers, 30 floor bands) with every row drawn: worker / child / floor band 43 / 20 / 28.5px wide, 87 / 46 / 55px in the phone grid (≤760px), child 64 and band 65px at ≤480px (a child's task wraps to its second line about there, a band's chips at some 400px); Ubuntu 46 / 24 / 30, 90 / 50 / 58, 69 / 69 (in its own block). A row drawn once keeps its own height. So the scrollbar keeps its length: scrolled top to bottom, the board's length stays within 1.0% of its fully drawn length in Quiet and Ubuntu at 1280×720, 600×844 and 390×844 (h145-overview-rows holds it to 3%); with round 1's one desktop estimate it was 2.2% / 5.8% off wide and 36–38% on a phone and the narrow grid (18,925 → 30,009px at 390, Quiet). Each kind's estimate is set again after `.ov-row` in every media block (all one class: the later rule wins). A row resized across 760px keeps a remembered height until it is drawn again. A skipped row's animations do not run (an animation it held while drawn stays, never advanced, styled or painted). Its paint is clipped: the glow (16px) and the ring (×2.4) fit inside the row at every width and theme (h145-overview-rows checks the geometry), and `overflow-clip-margin: border-box` lets the orchestrator's stub cross its row's rule as before. Rows of fractional height snap their contents to whole pixels (≤1px). No `will-change`: layers are the drawn rows' animations only. |
| 4 | Keys onto a skipped row | Focus and `scrollIntoView` make the row relevant: End on perf-floor60 lands on the last row focused, in view and drawn whole. `foldAway` reads its rows' sizes after all its writes (one layout; a skipped row reports its remembered size). |
| 5 | Opening again | The view the board last showed keeps its rows when the page closes; opening it again reconciles them by signature like any refresh (what changed while closed shows at once: no flash, fold or flip), restarts the skeletons the close stopped, and clears one-shot motion the hidden page cut short. Another view (`a`, or the other page) builds its own. The cascade and the grow play as before. **The scroll position behaves as before**: nothing writes `scrollTop`, so the board comes back where it was scrolled to (Chromium keeps a `display: none` box's offset, and the rows' remembered sizes survive it: the same rows are in view at 1280 and at 390px, Ubuntu), and the first row takes the focus without scrolling to it (off-screen, as on base); ArrowDown goes on to the second and scrolls it into view. `a` keeps the offset too, as it always did. Round 1 put the board back at its top: dropped (AC3). |
| 6 | Focus out of the key | The first row takes the focus on the frame the page first draws (`requestAnimationFrame`), whose layout is needed anyway, instead of forcing one inside the keydown; a key pressed before then keeps the focus it moved. |
| 7 | Measured (h145-overview-perf, this Linux host, headless Chromium, 1280×720, the scene stopped by a hidden-document counterfactual, base fea809e vs head interleaved, 2 runs each of 20 s idle and 15 s of wheel scrolling) | perf-floor60 idle: main thread 320–341 → 50–55 ms/s, style 100–131 → 18–19 ms/s, paints 2,191–2,218 → 0.1–0.2 /s (paint 168–180 → 0.1 ms/s), layers 62 → 27, endless animations drawn 42 → 16. perf-city240 idle: main thread 568–614 → 76–78 ms/s, style 358–367 → 23 ms/s, paints 2,908–2,923 → 0.1 /s, layers 104 → 31, animations 168 → 19. Scrolling: main thread 376–470 → 277–286 (floor60) and 766–825 → 386–388 ms/s (city240), paint about halved, frames over 25 ms 0–6 → 0 and 0–8 → 0 (p95 16.7 ms both). perf-floor96 open (5 runs each): the key's handler 75–81 → 15–37 ms on a first open (of it 22–25 ms → 0 of forced layout), 53–140 (median 60) → 3.5–14 (median 4.1) ms on an open again; from the key to the end of the first frame 96–104 → 67–71 ms on a first open in 3 runs (149–186 in 2, where the open follows the two pages before it; 66–69 ms in 6 cold opens apart), median 80 → 45 ms opening again. |
| 8 | The Mac | `H3D_PERF_JOBS=floor60-ov,city240-ov,floor96-ov pnpm perf:mac` (on the base build and on this one) runs the same page alone in the Mac's Chrome: main thread per second and per frame (that Chrome runs without vsync), layers, and the time from O to the end of the first frame, first and again. |

## 2026-10-20 — #141: floor entry stops rebuilding every office shader

Every elevator ride, floor switch and "go to worker" on another floor froze the page for one frame of 650–1100 ms on
this host: the new `OfficeView` was all new instanced meshes and new lamps, and the old one was disposed before the
new one drew. three r186 keys an `InstancedMesh`'s compiled state by its uuid and captures its instance buffers when it
builds it (`RenderObject.js:846-850`, `nodes/accessors/Instance.js`), and every lit material's state by the lights' ids
(`LightsNode.js:147-169`), so the first frame built the whole office's node graphs and programs again. Code:
`game/src/render/floorPool.ts` (`FloorPool`, `PoolKit`, `poolCapacity`, `reuse`, `meshKit`), the kits in `crowd.ts`,
`desks.ts`, `tray.ts`, `cards/atlasCards.ts`, `monitorCards.ts`, `screens.ts`, `props.ts` (plants), `rack.ts` (LEDs),
`boards/noteBoard.ts`; `office.ts` (`officeLamps`, `holdsPool`, `dispose`); `app.ts` (`retire`, `render`,
`keepOutside`, `enterFloor`, `warmUp`), `render/disposeHold.ts`; the probe `floorPoolProbe.ts` (`__h3d.floorPool`); specs
`e2e/h141-floor-entry.spec.ts`, `e2e/h141-floor-entry-perf.spec.ts`, `src/render/floorPool.test.ts`.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What is kept | **A pool of instanced meshes, one kit per part, outliving the offices** (`FloorPool`, owned by `App`). A kit is a part's instanced meshes with their geometry, material, per-instance attributes and atlas canvases (the crowd, the desks, the trays, the cards, the monitor cards, the frozen screens, the plants, the rack's LEDs, the two note boards). An office part takes its kit (`take(key, desks, holder, make)`) and writes its floor into it as a new mesh would be written: `count`, matrices, colours, attributes, a blank atlas. The office's other objects stay per office: their states are keyed by structure, not by object, and live on through the next office (row 3). |
| 2 | Why per uuid, and the rules | The key holds the uuid and the state holds that mesh's arrays, so a state is correct for one mesh only. **One live mesh per uuid; a kit's `instanceMatrix` / `instanceColor` attributes and arrays are never replaced; `instanceColor` exists from construction where a part uses colour; `count` never exceeds the capacity.** A pooled mesh, its material and geometry are never disposed by an office (`OfficeView.dispose`, `Crowd.dispose`, … skip them): only the pool disposes a kit, when it outgrows it. A part whose kit was taken by a newer office (`holder`) writes nothing to it, so the office you left cannot draw into the floor you are on. A uuid probe (the investigation's prototype: one uuid per mesh by position) was measured faster but binds one mesh's draws to another's buffers, and was not used. |
| 3 | Growth | Capacity in desks: `poolCapacity(need, had)`, a multiple of 16, and at least 1.5 × the kit it replaces, so a floor that outgrows a kit gets a new one (new meshes, new uuids, the old one disposed) a few times in a session at most. demo floors of 6–20 desks: 16 then 32; perf-floor60: 64. Fixed-size kits (plants 4, LEDs, notes) never grow. The capacity is baked into the shader (three's uniform path); the unused instances past `count` are not drawn. |
| 4 | The lamps | **The same two `SpotLight`s on every floor** (`FloorPool.lamps`), moved into each new office's root at the place they always had, their targets beside them; each office sets their position, target and intensity, and only the office they hang in can change them. Count, order and ids stay the same, so the lights' key does not change from floor to floor (M17 row 6 made the set constant within a floor). |
| 5 | Releasing the old office | **After the new office's first frame** (`App.retire`, `render`): an office left (a floor switch, the city, the lobby, a resize) is taken out of the scene and disposed once a floor frame with an office has drawn, so the states the two share keep a user. Two swaps before a frame both wait; offices left for the city wait until the next floor frame. The building's outside is kept while you are in the city and reused when you enter the same building (`keepOutside`): its custom node materials (baked street, panes, pools, doors) never share across instances. |
| 6 | A cold ride | **Built while the doors close, compiled before they open.** With no office loaded (the city, a lobby) and the doors in use, the office is built in a task right after the doors start to close (used if the floor still has the same desks and outline and no office was built since, else built again), and after the swap `renderer.compileAsync(walk.scene, fpCam)` compiles the scene object by object, yielding between them, with the frame loop held (the doors hide the canvas; never two offices or two lamp sets in the scene). Hidden and culled meshes of the office are shown and unculled for the moment the compile picks its objects (it does before its first `await`), so the crew's props and the trays come compiled too. `renderer.info.calls` is advanced first: three keeps the scene's cache key per render call (`NodeManager.getCacheKey`), and the lamps just came into the scene. The shadow pass is not compiled (three skips it in a precompile): the first frame, still behind the doors, builds it. **What the world disposes during the compile is released again after it** (`holdDisposals`, `render/disposeHold.ts`): the compile picks every object with its material at once and builds them in later yields, where world events still run (a floor resized: the kits it outgrows and the outside are disposed at once; a swapped logo, texture or material); three listens for an object's `dispose` only once it has built it, so what it built after the dispose was kept for good (a resize 6 → 35 desks during the compile kept 66 geometries, 4 textures, 65 render objects, 58 states, 57 pipelines). While the compile runs every `dispose` event is recorded (`EventDispatcher.prototype.dispatchEvent`, wrapped for that time only) and fired again once it is done, before a frame can draw (#146: compiles that overlap share one recording, kept until the last of them is done, and fired again then; row 6 there): it reaches only the listeners three added after the first one, so it releases exactly what the compile built of them. Chosen over holding the world's events (or only the structural ones) during the compile because the disposals that race it come from many places (the pool's growth, the outside, the laptops, logo, TV and whiteboard texture swaps), and over a disposal queue for the same reason; a material disposed and kept (three's reset idiom) loses its compiled state then and builds it on the first frame. A floor removed during the ride puts you out in the city once the doors are open (`syncWalk` waits for the ride, as it waits for a seat). A warm swap (an office loaded) stays one atomic swap. Without doors (tests, reduced motion, `__h3d.enterFloor`) nothing changes. |
| 7 | Measured (this host, Chromium WebGL2 over ANGLE/Vulkan, base `fea809e` against head, interleaved, `H3D_WORKERS=1`) | Three runs each, interleaved (base, head, ×3), load average 2–26: **a warm entry's first frame 736 ms → 66 ms** (medians of the runs' medians; every warm entry: 730 → 62.5 ms, the slowest 944 → 116 ms), **its longest frame 949 → 120 ms at most** (perf-floor60 826–944 → 67–83 ms). A cold ride through the doors: the longest frame while they are shut **1228–1259 → 223–286 ms**, the first frame as they open 33–50 → 17–33 ms, and they stay shut **1396 ms against 1540** (the long frame no longer holds them). A first entry without doors (tests, reduced motion) is unchanged: 965–1065 against 1010–1198 ms. Ten rides A → B → A: geometries 180, textures 45, render objects 283, states 188, pipelines 175 after every one. Left: the radio screen's shadow-pass state (one per entry), and a building's outside built again when you enter another building. |
| 8 | Revisit | When three ships PR #35007 (merged to `dev` 2026-10-19: instanced meshes share one state and read their own buffers at draw time), the uuid key goes and the pool can go with it; the deferred release and the cold compile stay useful. Do not upgrade three for it before a release has it. |
| 9 | Tests | `floorPool.test.ts`: random floor sequences (seeded) keep every kit's mesh, attributes and arrays unless it grows (then new uuids, the old one disposed), `count` within capacity, one uuid per live mesh, nothing pooled disposed by an office, the lamps the same objects at the same place; an office left behind writes nothing. `h141-floor-entry.spec.ts`: re-entries (through the city and floor to floor, a floor that outgrows the kits, an asleep floor, shadows on and off) compared with the same floor entered first on a new page, mesh by mesh (count, the matrices and colours in use, material, shadows, the lamps) and by screenshot, each mesh's render state reading its own arrays; live changes after a re-entry (an arrival, a leaver, a move, a resize, asleep, the plan); ten rides A → B → A with the renderer's memory, render objects, states and pipelines flat; a new page's first ride with the floor resized (the kits grow), asleep, or removed during the compile, against the same change once the doors are open (the renderer's memory after two more floors, the floor drawn as on a new page; removed: out in the city). `disposeHold.test.ts`. `h141-floor-entry-perf.spec.ts` (`@perf`). |

## 2026-10-21 — #138: Codex accounts are Codex home folders (profiles), not a switcher

Epic #135 asked for a Codex account switcher: one `~/.codex` whose `auth.json` codex-auth swaps for the whole host.
Research #136 (`docs/research/codex-accounts.md`) came back **NO-GO** on a global switch: every running Codex worker,
the shared app-servers and the limits probe read the one `auth.json`, so a swap moves them all at once, and its
recommendation is one Codex home per account. #137 (`docs/research/codex-accounts-shared-setup.md`) lists what a
second home lacks and how to share it. The user already runs `~/.codex` and `~/.codex-work` this way.

| # | Decision | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | An account is a profile, a profile is a folder | A Codex profile is a Codex home folder with its own sign-in. Nothing is switched: a profile is read (and, with #139, hired on) with `CODEX_HOME=<folder>`. No codex-auth. |
| 2 | Found, then edited | The bridge's own home (`$CODEX_HOME`, else `~/.codex`, the folder `--codex-sessions` defaults into) is the default; every `~/.codex-*` folder with an `auth.json` is found; the user adds other folders by path. In Settings → Codex profiles each can be named and hidden (not the default); an added one removed. Stored by the bridge (`codex_profiles_settings`, one JSON row). |
| 3 | `auth.json` is only stat'ed | Its existence finds a sibling and says "signed in"; it is never opened, logged, stored or sent. A reading with a plan also counts as signed in (Codex can keep the sign-in in the keyring). |
| 4 | Stable keys from the folder | `~/.codex` → `codex`, `~/.codex-work` → `work`; any folder that could share its name with another (elsewhere, `.codex-Work`, `~/.codex-codex`) adds a hash of its path (`/data/team-codex` → `team-codex-32b74a`). A key is the folder's alone: the first cut gave a collision `-2` in listing order, and a folder that went made the other take over its key, with its reading, plan and retry state (review R1). A hashed key and a folder's name never meet: a name that ends in `-` and 6 or more hex digits (`~/.codex-a-812dc0`, the hashed key of `~/.codex-+a`) is hashed too, and two paths whose 6 digits are the same both take all 64 (review round 3: the `-2` in listing order had stayed for that). The default name is the folder's name (`codex`, not "personal": the folder decides who it belongs to, not the bridge). A rename keeps the key; settings are stored by folder path. The hub lists the profiles again itself when the poller's list changed, so a list the poller took before a settings change never undoes it (review R3). |
| 5 | Limits per profile, keyed (provider, profile) | The poller probes each visible profile in turn with its own `CODEX_HOME` (an inherited one replaced), its own schedule and backoff, its transcript fallback in its own `sessions/` (the default's still `--codex-sessions`). Poller state, the hub's map and the snapshot are keyed by provider and profile key; readings carry `account {key, name, plan, default}`. Hidden profiles are not read. The profiles are listed again with the poll (every 2 minutes, and on `limits.refresh`), only while a client is connected; that is checked again before each profile's read, and one left unread when the last client goes stays due (review R2). |
| 6 | Old clients keep working | Readings keep `provider: "codex"`; an old client shows one Codex row (whichever came last). A reading without `account` is the default profile's. |
| 7 | The meter looks the same with one profile | Two or more Codex readings: one row each, named by profile, the default marked and first, then by name. One: "Codex" as before, no marker. The hire and start-run dialogs show the default profile's limits only, until #139 adds a picker. |
| 8 | Seam for #139 | `internal/codexaccount`: `Account`, the `Lister` interface (`Accounts(ctx)`) the poller reads through, and the `Service` that #139 extends with `Prepare(ctx, key)` (the env with `CODEX_HOME`). Out of scope here: hiring or waking on a profile, any switching, syncing skills or config between homes (a profile row is a column so per-profile options can go under it). |
| 9 | Tests | `go test ./internal/codexaccount ./internal/limits ./internal/server -run 'Codex|Profile|Limits'`; `world/limits.test.ts`, `ui/limits.profiles.dom.test.ts`, `ui/codexProfilesSection.dom.test.ts`, `tools/fixture-codex-profiles.test.ts`; the fixture's `simcodexprofiles=2` (CONTRIBUTING). |

## 2026-10-21 — #147: the bridge deflates its websocket (permessage-deflate, context takeover)

Every transcript's first-page ack (median 479 kB, largest 767 kB over the 64 private #126 acks), the start-up snapshot
and every reconnect crossed the SSH tunnel uncompressed: the bridge accepted websockets with nil options, and
coder/websocket's default is no compression. Code: `acceptOptions` (`internal/server/ws.go`); tests
`internal/server/compress_test.go`, `TestWSCompression` (`internal/helper/server_test.go`); benchmarks
`internal/server/compress_bench_test.go`.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Mode | **`websocket.CompressionContextTakeover`**, the library's superset: a client that offers only `client/server_no_context_takeover` gets that, one that offers nothing gets no compression. Chrome (the Mac's `--app` window) offers `permessage-deflate; client_max_window_bits` and gets context takeover both ways; the library's "Safari does not implement it" note does not apply. Go clients (`proto.Dial`, the codex-shared-bridge suite) dial with default options, offer nothing and are unchanged. The helper's proxy forwards the offer and the answer as they are (`Sec-WebSocket-Extensions` is end to end; `TestWSCompression` pins it). |
| 2 | Threshold | **The library's default, 128 B** (no `CompressionThreshold`). The writer level is fixed at `flate.BestSpeed` (the ticket's level-6 figure is not reachable). Over a burst of `worker.status` events (225 B each) context takeover sends **27 B** a message at 7.8–8.5 µs (0.73–0.75 µs uncompressed); a threshold of 512 or 1024 leaves them at 229 B. A watched transcript's live tail (each item of the median ack in a push of its own, 572 B mean): 158 B at 13–16 µs with 128, 286 B at 8–9 µs with 512, 297 B at 8–9 µs with 1024, 334 B at 7 µs without context takeover, 576 B at 0.5 µs off. At the bridge's message rates that is well under a millisecond of CPU a second per page, so the smaller messages are worth it where they come in bursts. |
| 3 | Measured: acks (`BenchmarkDeflateAcks`, the 64 dumps as `transcript.watch` acks, Chrome's offer, bytes the bridge writes) | **30.23 MB → 8.37 MB (3.61×)**; median ack 478.6 → **134.1 kB**, largest 767.2 → **203.6 kB**. Without context takeover 8.39 MB (3.60×): on big messages the two modes are the same, the window pays on small ones (row 2). |
| 4 | Measured: CPU per ack (`BenchmarkDeflateAckWrite`, the bridge's `ws.Write` on a connection that drops what it is given, this host, i7-10750H at load 6–7) | Median ack **4.8–5.0 ms**, largest **7.5–8.2 ms** (≈ 95–103 MB/s), 0 allocs/op (5–10 kB/op amortized from the library's pools). Uncompressed the write is under 1 µs there (no copy). The write runs on the connection's own writer goroutine (`serveWS`), not on the hub's. |
| 5 | Memory | Per connection that negotiated it: the `flate.Writer` (BestSpeed: **486 kB** measured on Go 1.27; the library's comment says 1.2 MB), made at the first compressed message (the snapshot) and kept for the connection's life, plus a 32 kB window for the client's own deflated messages and a pooled 45 kB reader while reading one. **About 0.5 MB per open page**; the bridge holds one websocket per open page (a page or two on the Mac), and Go clients negotiate nothing. |
| 6 | Read limit | `ws.SetReadLimit(maxClientMsg)` bounds a client's message as inflated (the limit reader wraps the flate reader), so a small deflated message that inflates past 256 KiB is still refused with "message too big" (`TestWebSocketCompressedReadLimit`). |
| 7 | The real browser | Chromium 149 (Playwright) through the helper's own handler (`helper.NewServer`, its `/ws` proxy and checks) on 127.0.0.1, the bridge on a local socket (no SSH tunnel), a page that says hello and reads the snapshot of a floor of 2000 workers: CDP `Network.webSocketHandshakeResponseReceived` shows `Sec-WebSocket-Extensions: permessage-deflate`; the 833.8 kB snapshot arrived whole, and the helper wrote **133.4 kB** on the browser's connection (834.1 kB on the base commit, which negotiates nothing). CDP's `webSocketFrameReceived` shows the inflated payload, so it cannot measure the wire. |
| 8 | Not measured | **The end-to-end saving over the real SSH tunnel is still an estimate** (the ticket's 40–90 ms per open from fewer slow-start round trips at 23 ms RTT, more on a thin uplink). To be confirmed on the Mac after deploy: `transcript.watch` → ack time, before and after. |

## 2026-10-21 — #163: a prefixless random token is proposed (the entropy rule)

A real, revoked 64-letter mixed-case API token, typed as `Actually, token is this one: <value>` into a hire prompt, got
no review: Gitleaks' `generic-api-key` drops a value of letters only (its allowlist `^[a-zA-Z_.-]+$`) and the prose rule
reads `this`, not the value after `is this one:`. Not fixed with phrases or languages, nor by touching an allowlist: a
language-independent candidate for a random-looking word, next to the others (from #150's research). Code:
`internal/promptsecret/entropy.go` (`entropySpans`, the word and the exclusions), `scan.go` (`detect`, `entropyKept`,
the repeat step), `structural.go` (`KindEntropy`'s rank), `review.go` (`scanBytesUnder`); the protocol's kinds in
`docs/protocol.md` "Prompt secrets" and `game/src/net/protocol.ts` (`SecretCandidate.kinds`); no client change.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | What it is | A new kind, **`entropy`**, found with the same switch as every other detector (it runs inside the one `Scan`, so `Reviewer.Scan`, `Check` and `CheckScan`, the preview and the send-time rescan agree, on every #108 route). A candidate is a **whole word** of **32 to 512 bytes** whose Shannon entropy is **at least 4.5 bits per byte** and that looks random. Nothing is protected or ignored for the user; a candidate goes through the same protect / ignore / correct review. |
| 2 | The lexical run | One maximal run of `[A-Za-z0-9]` and `_ - + /` (base64, url-safe base64, snake and kebab case), plus up to two `=` right after it as base64 padding when no run byte and no other `=` follows them. An `=` followed by a run byte (`API_KEY=<tok>`, `a==b`) ends the run and is never in it. The candidate is exactly the typed bytes (padding included); no decoding, no normalizing; a non-ASCII byte (a letter, a combining mark, punctuation, an emoji, a CJK character) is never in a run and is a boundary. Length and entropy are measured without the padding. A combining mark glued after an ASCII letter leaves that typed letter in the run. |
| 3 | The word | The run is a candidate only when it is the whole word. Before it: the text's start, a blank, a quote or backtick, one of `( [ { < > , ; : = \| *`, a non-ASCII byte, or a JSON-escaped `\n`, `\r`, `\t` glued before it (that escape letter is not part of the run). After it: the end, a blank, a quote, one of `) ] } > , ; * \| <`, a non-ASCII byte, a `\` before `n r t` or a quote, or sentence punctuation (`. : ! ?`, any run of it) that is followed by one of those and never by a word byte. So `API_KEY=<tok>`, `token:<tok>`, `"<tok>"`, `'<tok>'`, `` `<tok>` ``, `(<tok>)`, `<tok>.`, `<tok>,`, `<tok>!`, `<tok>?`, `<tok>;`, `**<tok>**`, `<code><tok></code>` propose exactly `<tok>`, and `<tok>.png`, `<tok>.example.org`, `<tok>?page=2`, `<tok>:8080`, `<tok>(x)`, `<tok>[0]`, `<tok>@host`, `www.<tok>`, `%2F<tok>`, `$<tok>`, `#<tok>`, `C:\\x\\<tok>` propose nothing. A URL is one word (a `://` earlier in the same blank-or-quote delimited piece, or a piece that starts `//` after a scheme's colon) and so is a `data:` URI (`;base64,` before the run, or a `data:` piece): nothing inside is proposed. **A run over 512 bytes is one long word and proposes nothing, never a plausible substring of it** (a 600-byte run, the same split by a `.`, 513 bytes: nothing; 512: proposed). The bytes of an own file reference are boundaries and never part of a run (row 7). |
| 4 | Entropy: formula and numbers | The formula is `gitleaks.go`'s `shannonEntropy` (each symbol's frequency over the length, `log2`: "upstream's rune-over-byte formula") computed over bytes; a run is ASCII, so bytes and runes agree (`TestByteEntropyIsGitleaksFormula`). **Window 32–512 and 4.5 bits kept**, as measured. Seeded random tokens, 2,000 per cell, share under 4.5 bits: letters (52 symbols) 57.7 % at 32 bytes, 10.8 % at 40, 0.6 % at 48, **0 at 64 and 128**; letters and digits 33.2 % / 2.5 % / 0.1 % / 0 / 0; base64 with `+/` 30.6 % / 1.6 % / 0.1 % / 0 / 0; one-case letters (26 symbols) 93.3 % at 64 and 11.1 % at 128; hex never reaches 4.0 at any length (16 symbols), so hex SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512, git ids and UUIDs fall short by themselves (`TestEntropyNegatives` asserts it for 32 to 512 bytes). So a 32- or 40-byte token of letters is often missed (the price of the threshold) and a lowercase-only one needs about 128 bytes. A lower threshold was measured on the repo corpus and refused: at 4.0 bits the scan adds about 260 candidates over the corpus of row 9, nearly all CamelCase Go test names (`TestFooBarBaz…`), `msg_…` ids and long identifiers, which sit between 4.0 and 4.5 bits; at 4.5 none. |
| 5 | What is excluded, and how | Not random whatever the entropy: a repeated block (shortest period at most half the run: KMP), a run in which a quarter of the neighbouring bytes are consecutive (`abcdef…`, `0123…`, the alphabet), a placeholder or redaction the alphabet can spell (`your-…`, `…_here`, `replace-…`, `insert-…`, `enter-…`, `redacted`). Public or structured, by what starts or surrounds the run: **SSH public keys** (the type word before it: `ssh-rsa`, `ssh-ed25519`, `ecdsa-sha2-…`, `sk-…`; or the blob's own start, `AAAAB3NzaC1`, `AAAAC3NzaC1`, `AAAAE2VjZHNh…`, the `sk-` ones), **SRI and lockfile hashes** (`sha1-` … `sha512-`, `sha3-N-`, `md5-`, `blake2…-` start), **go.sum and Nix hashes** (the words `h1`, `hash`, `sha256`, `checksum`, `digest`, `integrity`, `fingerprint`, `etag`, `commit`, `uuid`, `guid` right before: the last word that is no filler such as `is` or `the`), **build ids** (`<build|trace|span|request|correlation|image|container|commit|revision|release|run|job|pipeline|deployment|instance> id` right before), **public keys** (`public` among the last three non-filler words, unless a credential word (`api`, `token`, `secret`, `password`, `access`, `auth`, `credential`, `private`, `session`, `login`, and Dutch, French, German and Spanish ones: `sleutel`, `wachtwoord`, `clé`, `jeton`, `schlüssel`, …; never `key` alone) stands between `public` and the run or within two words before `public`: `my public key: <b64>` and `my public ssh key: <b64>` are out, `my public API key <tok>`, `Use the public API token <tok>`, `API key public: <tok>` and `my public repo's token <tok>` are proposed; the other words (hash, digest, checksum, commit, h1, `<build|run|…> id`) are read only as the nearest word, so `the build token <tok>`, `commit token <tok>`, `the deployment key is <tok>`, `job password <tok>` and `pipeline API key <tok>` name a credential and are proposed; `TestEntropyContextWordsDoNotHideACredential` runs 15 introductions × 29 context words × 6 to 10 positions × 6 separators × 2 tokens, `TestEntropyPublicContextStillExcludes` the reverse; round 2 of the review, R2), **PEM bodies** of every block that is no private key (BEGIN to END, or to a blank line when unclosed; a private key's lines stay proposed, the `pem` rule wins a whole block), **paths and slugs** (a `/` and most bytes in segments of one case, or a root path starting with a plain directory: `/tmp/…`, `/nix/store/…`, `src/fonts/x/X-LICENSE`), **URLs and data URIs** (row 3). The bypass this opens is deliberate and small: a real token typed right after `hash`, `public key`, `build id`… is not proposed; every other word keeps the rule. |
| 6 | With the other detectors | The entropy rule **adds where nothing else found a byte** (`entropyKept`): an entropy span overlapping any other span is dropped, so every provider, structural and generic finding keeps its bytes and its kinds (an identical range adds no kind: `TestScanFamilies`, `TestScanRecall`, `TestScanBoundaries`, `TestScanOverlaps`, the reference tests, `TestScanCleanText` pass unchanged). One exception, shown on the corpus: a **Gitleaks generic finding is no known format**, only a value after a name, and its alphabet includes `.` and `=`, so `Actually, token is this one: <tok>.` and `secret_value=<tok>. Thanks` proposed `<tok>.` with the sentence's period (and its repeat the same); the run replaces the generic span at its exact bytes (rank `entropy` before `generic`; `TestEntropyReplacesAGenericValue`) **only when the bytes the generic finding has outside the run are the sentence's punctuation after it** (`. ! ? :`; the same start, nothing before, nothing else after). Every other overlap keeps the generic finding whole, as on base, and drops the run: a prefix (`foo=<tok>`: the run starts after the `=`, and protecting only it would leave `foo=` in the prompt and change the credential; review round 2, R1), a longer value (`<tok>-suffix`, `<tok>.<tok2>`), a generic span inside the run, a partial overlap. `foo=<tok>.` is decided as base has it: the finding is the whole value including the period, and it is the candidate (trimming only the period would be a second rule for a case in which the run does not own the start; the period is inside a credential only the user can judge). `TestEntropyKeepsAGenericFinding` runs 14 name phrasings × 13 value shapes × 11 trailers × 2 leads and asserts every generic finding keeps every byte except that trailing punctuation, with sorted, non-overlapping, byte-exact candidates; `TestEntropyGenericWithAPrefix` pins `foo=<tok>`, `foo=<tok>.`, `foo=<tok>...`. Another occurrence of a value another rule found stays a `repeat` as before (the entropy spans are not read for repeats and give way to one: `TestEntropyComposition`); the occurrences of a value only the entropy rule found are each their own `entropy` candidate. A credential-named assignment keeps its own boundary: `API_KEY=<tok>!` and `token: <tok>?` propose `<tok>!` / `<tok>?` as before (a password may end in `!`); the matrix asserts exactly that. |
| 7 | Own references | The rule reads typed bytes only: each own file reference is a boundary and never part of a run (the masked pass runs the rule too, over the same text with the reference bytes skipped, so it finds what the typed pass finds and the mask's spelling never completes a length or a case), so an entropy span never overlaps a reference, is never `shaped` and so never `borrowed`. A token before, after, between or beside references is proposed at its typed bytes (`TestEntropyOwnReferences`); a reference's own path words are never proposed (a span inside one reference is dropped as for every detector, and the path is no candidate by row 5 anyway); text that only looks like a reference is scanned as any text. |
| 8 | Stale reviews | `RulesVersion` is now `gitleaks-v8.30.1+structural-1+entropy-1`, so every revision and stored digest made before is stale. `TestRevisionOfTheOldRulesIsStale` builds the revision a review made under the old version had and shows `Check` and `CheckScan` refuse it as stale (and that a stored digest follows the version). `Reviewer.Scan`, `Check` and `CheckScan` keep going through the one `Scan`. A schedule or preset saved before is not rescanned until it is saved again; its fire rescans and fails as an unreviewed prompt when the new rule finds something (round 2 row 19). A Telegram reply holding a long random word is now refused with the fixed sentence (round 1 row 14) instead of sent. |
| 9 | Measured: the repo corpus (AC3) | `Scan(chunk, nil)` over 16 KiB chunks of every tracked `.md .go .ts .sh .yml .json` file (not `node_modules`, not `gitleaks_rules.go`; files this change edits left out) and every `/usr/share/doc/**/README*`: **1,894 files, 26.3 MB**; base `a47f1d4` 2,244 candidates, head 2,337: **93 new** and 2 boundary fixes (`k3jd…6ure` against `k3jd…ure.`, the generic finding and its repeat that held the period); 0 kind changes. **Zero new candidates in any source, doc or README outside the test fixtures and the research corpora**: 81 in `docs/research/prompt-secret-bench/**`, `tools/secretrules/testdata/corpus.json` and the holdout report (34 distinct values, each one of the corpus' labeled synthetic secrets, in 5 copies of the corpus), 12 in test fixtures (a Telegram bot token's tail in `notify_test.go` and `telegramSection.dom.test.ts`, an OAuth value and PEM-body lines in `handoffllm/scrub_test.go`, synthetic tokens in `structural_test.go`). By class: true-secret-looking 81 + 12, SSH key 0, SRI hash 0, PEM 0 (the `scrub_test.go` lines are private-key-shaped fixtures), `data:` URI 0, build id or digest 0, other 0. Without the exclusions of row 5 the same scan adds 16 more: 6 SSH public key blobs (`AAAA…woGO`, 68 bytes), 1 SRI `sha512-…==`, 1 go.sum `h1:…=`, 1 base64 HTML fixture, 5 paths (`src/fonts/excalidraw/EXCALIDRAW-LICENSE`, four 116–155 byte `/tmp/…` paths), 2 YouTube playlist ids in a URL (`/usr/share/doc/yt_dlp/README.txt`): each class is excluded by a named rule and asserted in `TestEntropyNegatives` / `TestEntropyWords`. Accepted noise, asserted in `TestEntropyAcceptedNoise`: a random-looking word with nothing around it that says what it is (a bare build id `artifact <40 random>`, a base64 payload line, an opaque id): proposed, the review decides. On #150's own 30 clean controls the union flagged 10/30; this rule's own noise on ordinary prompts, prose and code is none in 26 MB. |
| 10 | Measured: recall (AC1) | The generated matrix (`TestEntropyMatrix`: 9 token families (64 and 128 letters, 64 alphanumerics, base64 with `+/`, padded `==` and `=`, url-safe, edge symbols) × 30 layouts (none, English, Dutch, French and German introductions, quotes, backticks, parentheses, brackets, `API_KEY=`, `token:`, `export X=`, JSON, YAML, a fence, Markdown, accents, CJK, emoji, `«»`, curly quotes, an ellipsis, JSON-escaped newlines) × 13 trailers (none, `. , ! ? ) ; " : ...`, LF, CRLF, more text) = 3,510 cases, each asserting the one candidate at the exact `[Start, End)`): **base 865/3,510 (the ones an existing rule found; 65 of 390 for 64 letters), head 3,510/3,510**. Layouts the rule cannot satisfy: only that a credential-named assignment (`API_KEY=`, `token:`, `- token:`) keeps its `!` or `?` (row 6). Pilot corpus (`tools/secretrules` `TestScanOnThePilotCorpus`): exact 34/36 → **35/36**, partial 0, missed 2 → 1, clean prompts flagged 1/22 both. |
| 11 | Measured: time (AC4) | Interleaved base and head test binaries, 9 rounds each, 300 ms per benchmark, on a shared host (the best of 9 is the comparable figure: best-of differs by 0.5 ms or less on every row but the long-token ones, whose head medians sit about 5 ms above base at 16 and 32 KiB, with noisier rounds); `BenchmarkScan16KiB` 27.21 → 27.20 ms best (27.84 → 28.48 median); `BenchmarkScanSizes` (prose / prose with long tokens / near-misses it reads and drops), best base → head: 8 KiB 6.03 → 6.12 / 16.35 → 16.87 / 14.77 → 14.83 ms, 16 KiB 11.90 → 12.02 / 32.87 → 33.28 / 29.17 → 29.43 ms, **32 KiB 24.32 → 24.18 / 65.28 → 68.15 / 59.06 → 59.51 ms**. The entropy pass alone (`BenchmarkEntropySpans`, 32 KiB): prose 0.13 ms, near-misses 0.21 ms, **400 long tokens (every 80 bytes) 2.2 ms**; a byte scan with no regexp on the hot path (a regexp per qualifying run cost 12.9 ms there: the first cut, replaced by `placeholderRun`). An earlier noisy round (host loaded, swings of 30 to 50 %) showed the same within the noise. `TestScanTimeSizes` keeps every size and shape under 2 s. |
| 12 | Tests | `internal/promptsecret`: `TestEntropyMatrix` (above), `TestEntropyPadding`, `TestEntropyAdjacency` (two, repeated and three values with 11 separators), `TestEntropyOffsets` (UTF-16 range after astral characters), `TestEntropyWords` (43 word, URL, data URI, limit and escape layouts), `TestEntropyUnicodeBoundaries`, `TestEntropyNegatives` (hex, UUIDs, git ids, SSH keys of four types, SRI, go.sum, Nix, PEM public, certificate and request blocks, `data:` URIs, build, run and image ids, ETags, Nix store paths, CI run numbers, placeholders, masks, repeated and sequential strings, identifiers, paths, URLs, JWT-like words, long words), `TestEntropyAcceptedNoise`, `TestEntropyComposition`, `TestEntropyReplacesAGenericValue`, `TestEntropyKeepsAGenericFinding`, `TestEntropyGenericWithAPrefix`, `TestEntropyContextWordsDoNotHideACredential`, `TestEntropyPublicContextStillExcludes`, `TestEntropyPublicAPIWording`, `TestEntropyOwnReferences`, `TestEntropyScanInvariants` (300 seeded mixes: sorted, never overlapping, on character boundaries, deterministic), `TestByteEntropyIsGitleaksFormula`, `TestRevisionOfTheOldRulesIsStale`, `TestScanTimeSizes`, `BenchmarkScanSizes`, `BenchmarkEntropySpans`. `internal/server`: `TestPromptSecretsEntropyHire` (`worker.hire`: refused without a review, a reference with the exact bytes in the worker's file, ignored as typed), `TestPromptSecretsEntropyHireInterpret` (a dictated hire: the model reads a reference), `TestPromptSecretsEntropySchedule` (a stored prompt), `TestPromptSecretsEntropyPrompt` (`worker.prompt`). All tokens are generated from seeds; none is a real token or carries a vendor prefix. |

## 2026-10-21 — hire presets pinned to the desk tabs

With many hire presets, hiring one was the Hire preset tab, a search down the list, then Use. A preset can now be
**pinned**: it gets its own tab in the desk dialogs' tab bar, after Hire worker, Hire orchestrator and Hire preset, and
one click opens its hire form, ready to Hire. Code: `ui/hirePins.ts` (the pins and `deskPins`, a floor's tab bar), `ui/deskTabs.ts` (the
pinned tabs, their drag and Shift+← / Shift+→), the Pin button and `usePinned` of `ui/hirePresets.ts`, and the tab bars
of `ui/hire.ts` and `ui/startRun.ts`. Tests: `ui/hirePins.test.ts`, `ui/deskTabs.dom.test.ts`,
`ui/hirePresets.dom.test.ts`, `ui/hire.preset.dom.test.ts`, the pins test of `e2e/h93-hire-presets.spec.ts`, and the
`hire-presets` / `hire-pinned` surfaces of `e2e/ui-surfaces.ts`.

| # | Question | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Where pins live | **Per browser**, in local storage scoped to the bridge (`h3d.hire.pinnedPresets`, like Settings → Harness models): an ordered list of preset ids. Nothing on the bridge, no protocol change. Pins do not follow the player to another device; a later `pin_order` column on `hire_preset` would. |
| 2 | Which pins a tab bar shows | The pinned presets the floor offers (its own and the global ones), in pin order. Another floor's pin waits for its floor. A preset deleted (here, on another client, or while this browser was away) is unpinned on the next world change once the bridge has sent its presets (`HirePins.prune`). The tabs follow renames and deletions live. |
| 3 | What a pinned tab does | What Use does: the hire form for the desk with the preset's prompt and exact choice, ready to Hire. A desk with an unsent first task opens the preset list asking first (Keep my task / Replace it). The form shows that pinned tab as selected; Hire worker goes back to the desk's own form. |
| 4 | Pinning | A Pin toggle (`aria-pressed`) on each row of the preset list; a new pin goes at the end. |
| 5 | Moving | Only the pins move, never the three fixed tabs: drag a pin before or after another (a bar marks where it lands), or Shift+← / Shift+→ on a focused pin (focus stays on it). Alt+arrows stay the browser's Back and Forward. A move among one floor's pins keeps the places of the pins hidden there. The shortcut is in the pinned tab's tooltip, not the shortcut list: that list allows one binding per chord in dialogs, and the secrets review owns Shift+← / Shift+→. |
| 6 | Look | A push-pin icon, the name cut at 13 rem with the preset's choice as the tooltip, after a thin divider; the bar wraps to a second row when the pins do not fit. Below 480 px the pins take a row of their own under the three fixed tabs. |
